title: Military Engagements in Spanish, Mexican & Conquest-Era California
subtitle: Battles, raids, revolts, and standoffs, 1769–1848 — from the military register
abstract: Every engagement plotted here is documented in the project's military register, compiled from the C-A transcripts (Archives of California), Bancroft, Cook, and printed primary collections. Hollow or dashed markers mean the location is approximate or conjectural — the source names a district, not a spot. Register numbers (#) key each pin to the register's fuller entry and sources.

features.name: Battle at San Diego Mission
features.summary: First armed clash in Alta California. Spanish exploring party attacked at Cosoy. 1 Spaniard killed (blacksmith José Manuel Robles), 3 natives killed.

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. I (1542–1800) (San Francisco: History Company, 1886), 137–39 — the attack of 15 August 1769 on the camp/mission at Cosoy.
San Diego, Libro de Misión, MS., 65 (mission register; Bancroft's manuscript authority for the identity of the man killed).
Francisco Palóu, Relación histórica de la vida... de Junípero Serra (Mexico, 1787), 84 — reports earlier assaults, 12–13 Aug. 1769.
NO Archives of California record attests this engagement. [null result, recorded deliberately]

features.notes: TWO FACTUAL PROBLEMS IN THE MAP TEXT, flagged not silently reconciled. (1) The map says the Spaniard killed was 'blacksmith José Manuel Robles'. Bancroft (I:138) says the blacksmith was WOUNDED and 'greatly distinguishes himself by his bravery, fighting without the protection of a cuera'; the man KILLED was a boy servant, and Bancroft's footnote 28, citing San Diego, Lib. Mis., MS., 65, names him 'a Spanish arriero 20 years old named José María Vegerano'. No source I consulted names any 'Robles'. The San Diego blacksmith named 'José Manuel' in Bancroft is Arroyo, who was killed in the DIFFERENT event of Nov. 1775 (feature reg-2) — the map appears to have imported the 1775 blacksmith's death into the 1769 entry. (2) Bancroft's wounded are Padre Vizcaíno, the blacksmith, a soldier and a Baja California Indian; '3 natives killed' matches Bancroft. RECOMMEND correcting the summary. Nearest C-A record in date/place is ca62-d20 (Cañizares's copy of Rivera y Moncada's 1769 diary), but that diary CLOSES 3 July 1769, six weeks before the attack, so it is not an attestation and I have deliberately not linked it.

features.name: Destruction of San Diego Mission
features.summary: 800–1,000 attackers from 9+ rancherías; dual-axis plan (mission + presidio). Defenders: Cpl. Rocha + 3 soldiers, 2 friars, 3 artisans = 11 men. Padre Jayme martyred (18 arrow wounds). Blacksmith Arroyo killed. Carpenter Urselino died of wounds. Cpl. Rocha fired muskets all night from adobe enclosure.
features.result: INDIGENOUS TACTICAL VICTORY — first successful mission destruction

quote.es: "Amad á Dios, hijos" — Jayme's last words. Urselino left his pay "for the benefit of his murderers."

sources.citation: Tte. José Francisco de Ortega to Tte.-Col. Juan Bautista de Anza, San Diego, 30 Nov. 1775, 'Expediente de investigación' on the burning of Mission San Diego and the death of Fr. Luis Jayme (certified copy by Capt. Fernando de Rivera y Moncada) — Prov. St. Pap., Benicia Mil. (C-A 15), orig. pp.1–7 / Savage pp.2–9, scan n2–n8, Doc 1.

Comandante Fernando de Rivera y Moncada and Sgt. Mariano Carrillo, expediente on an Indian conspiracy which uncovered the confessions to the Nov. 1775 revolt, San Diego, 10 Aug.–4 Sept. 1776 — Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 1), tomo i. 221–232 / Savage pp.526–539, scan n223–n234, Doc 100.

Capt. Fernando de Rivera y Moncada, interrogation of the imprisoned leaders of the San Diego revolt, San Diego, 31 May–18 June 1776 — Prov. St. Pap., Benicia Mil. (C-A 15), orig. pp.327–343 / Savage pp.24–25, scan n23–n24, Doc 28.

Tte. José Francisco de Ortega, interrogation of 'el indio Carlos', capitán of the mission ranchería and principal ringleader of the 5 Nov. 1775 revolt, declarations of 11, 13 and 15 Apr. 1776 — Prov. St. Pap., Benicia Mil. (C-A 15), orig. pp.294–327 / Savage p.24, scan n23, Doc 27.
Fr. Vicente Fuster, Registro de Defunciones / San Diego, Libro de Misión, MS., 74–75 (eyewitness burial entries for Fr. Luis Jayme, the mason Arroyo and the carpenter Urselino).
Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, I:249–54 ('Destruction of San Diego').

features.notes: Date/casualty checks against the manuscript: ca15-d1 gives the attack as the night of 5 Nov. 1775 (the map's 5 November is right; the catalog headline reads '4–5 Nov'). DISCREPANCY ON THE TRADES: the map says 'Blacksmith Arroyo killed. Carpenter Urselino died of wounds.' Ortega's informe as catalogued calls Manuel Arroyo a MASON (albañil) killed and Felipe Romero a mason wounded, while Bancroft I:250 calls Arroyo and Romero both BLACKSMITHS sleeping in the smithy. Both agree Urselino was the carpenter and died of his wounds (buried 10 Nov). I am not reconciling this — flagging it. Also: the manuscript names the wounded escort as cabo Rocha[?], Alejo Antonio Gonzáles, Juan Álvarez and Joaquín Armenta, which supports the map's 'Cpl. Rocha'. The map's '13+ rancherías' figure belongs properly to feature reg-63, which is the same leaf.

features.name: Carrillo's Punishment at Alocuachomi
features.summary: Punitive raid near San Juan Capistrano. 3 natives killed.

sources.citation: Cabo [Guillermo] Carrillo to Sgt. Francisco de Aguiar, report of the punitive expedition to the ranchería de Alocuachomi, 20 June 1777 — State Papers, Sacramento (C-A 55), Savage pp.49–51 (stamp 276), scan n275, Doc 327.
Auto of Sgt. Francisco de Aguiar ordering the attack, Misión y escolta de San Juan Capistrano, 19 June 1777 — State Papers, Sacramento (C-A 55), Savage pp.47–49 (stamp 274), scan n273, Doc 326.

Tte. José Francisco de Ortega, sumaria taken by Sgt. Francisco de Aguiar on the disorders in the San Juan Capistrano and San Gabriel escorts, 11 July 1777 (sumaria opened 26 May) — State Papers, Sacramento (C-A 55), scan n?, Doc 318.

Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, I:314 — 'in June 1777 the Alocuachomi rancheria threatened the neophytes of San Juan Capistrano, and Corporal Guillermo Carrillo was sent with five men to chastise the offenders, which he did by killing three and wounding several.'

features.notes: The manuscript refines the map on two points. (1) COMMANDER: the officer who led the raid was Cabo GUILLERMO Carrillo, not Sgt. Mariano Carrillo; the catalog marks the authorship of ca55-d327 as inferred, but Bancroft I:314 independently names 'Corporal Guillermo Carrillo... sent with five men', and ca55-d326 records Sgt. Aguiar ordering 'Cabo Guillermo Carrillo + 5 soldiers to attack the rancheria' — three-way agreement. Consider retitling the feature 'Guillermo Carrillo's punishment at Alocuachomi'. (2) CASUALTIES: the map's '3 natives killed' is defensible but soft — the report says 'tumbamos unos tres, dos quedaron en el sitio y el otro cayó en el agua dentro del tule' (about three brought down; two dead on the spot, the third fell into the water in the tules), plus two more who fled badly wounded and two taken prisoner, one of whom got 25 lashes. Bancroft rounds this to 'killing three and wounding several'. (3) The ranchería is spelled Alocuachomi in the raid report (ca55-d327) but Alamachomi in the order of the previous day (ca55-d326) — same place, Savage's reading varies. Exact date of the raid: 20 June 1777.

features.name: Ambush at San Juan (Briones killed)
features.summary: Midnight ambush near San Diego. Corporal Briones killed.

sources.citation: Tte. José Francisco de Ortega, diligencias on the death of Cabo Garci [Brito] Murillo, with inventory of his goods, relaying Sgt. Carrillo's report of the assault on the despatch party, San Diego, 17 Aug. 1777 — State Papers, Sacramento (C-A 55), orig. tomo vii, pp.~166–199 / Savage pp.199–200, scan n198–n199, Doc 231.

Tte. José Francisco de Ortega, instructions to Sgt. Mariano Carrillo for a punitive campaign against the gentiles who killed Cabo Briones; Carrillo's operations report rendered 9 Oct. 1777 — State Papers, Sacramento (C-A 55), orig. tomo vii, pp.200–216 / Savage p.201, scan n200, Doc 233.
Gov. Felipe de Neve to the Comandante General, 15 Apr. 1778 — Provincial Records (C-A 22), orig. pp.184–185 / Savage p.97, scan n97, Doc 124.
Gov. Felipe de Neve to the Comandante General, 16 Oct. 1778 — Provincial Records (C-A 22), orig. pp.192–193 / Savage p.98, scan n98, Doc 127.

Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, I:315 — 'on August 13th four soldiers bearing despatches from General Croix to Neve were surprised at midnight, at a place called San Juan just above San Diego... who killed the corporal in command, Antonio Briones.'

features.notes: THE MAP'S PLACE IS RIGHT BUT AMBIGUOUS AND THE CATALOG IS PROBABLY WRONG ABOUT IT. Bancroft I:315 puts the ambush 'at a place called San Juan just above San Diego', and ca22-d127 names it precisely: the rancherías of the ARROYO DE SAN JUAN BAUTISTA. The catalog summary of ca55-d233 glosses it as 'the gentiles of San Juan [Capistrano]' — that bracketed expansion looks like an editorial error, since San Juan Capistrano is ~60 miles north of San Diego and the party was returning FROM San Diego. Recommend the map say 'Arroyo de San Juan Bautista, above San Diego' and not San Juan Capistrano. SECOND FLAG — A DATE CONTRADICTION INSIDE THE ARCHIVE: ca55-d231 is dated 17 Aug. 1777 yet its Savage abstract says the assault happened 'on ~13 Oct'; that is internally impossible (a 17 August document cannot report a 13 October event). ca22-d124 (Neve, 15 Apr. 1778) and Bancroft both give 13 AUGUST 1777, which the 17 August dateline supports. I read this as a Savage or cataloguing slip for '13 Ago'. Do not silently correct in the catalog without a leaf check. THIRD: the corporal's full name is José Antonio Briones (Bancroft gives 'Antonio Briones'); the two wounded soldiers were Felipe Santiago Tapia and Joaquín Díaz, and the caballada was driven off.

features.name: Carrillo's Raid on Pamó
features.summary: Dawn assault on Pamó ranchería. 4 chiefs executed — first public execution in California.

sources.citation: Comte. Tte. José Francisco de Ortega, expediente on the Pamó conspiracy, the surprise of the ranchería (31 Mar. 1778) and the sentence of the four captains, San Diego, 6 Apr. 1778 — Prov. St. Pap., Benicia Mil. (C-A 15), orig. pp.737–764, 767–769 / Savage pp.43–46, scan n42–n45, Doc 46.

Tte. José Francisco de Ortega to Gov. Felipe de Neve, report that the four Pamó ringleaders have been shot, San Diego, 12 Apr. 1778 — Prov. St. Pap., Benicia Mil. (C-A 15), orig. pp.765–767 / Savage p.46, scan n45, Doc 47.
Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, I:315–16 — the Pamó campaign, Ortega's sentence quoted in translation, and Bancroft's judgement that 'This was the first public execution in California.'

features.notes: DATE CORRECTION FROM THE MANUSCRIPT: the map dates the feature to March 1778, which is right for the raid but the manuscript is precise — Sgt. Mariano Carrillo surprised Pamó at 3 a.m. on 31 MARCH 1778; the four captains were examined and convicted on 4–6 April; the executions were on SATURDAY 11 APRIL 1778, and Ortega reported them carried out on 12 April. So 'March 1778' should probably become '31 March – 11 April 1778'. SECOND: the map says '4 chiefs executed — first public execution in California.' The 'first public execution' claim is BANCROFT'S judgement (I:316), not the manuscript's; it should be attributed to him rather than presented as a fact of record. The four captains are Achil, Aalcuirin[?], Aarán and Taguaqui[?] (Bancroft: Aachil, Aalcuirin, Aaaran, Taguagui). THIRD: casualties in the raid itself were 2 killed outright plus an unspecified few burned in a hut they refused to leave. FOURTH, a related record I deliberately did NOT link: ca1-d126 (Ortega, Prov. St. Pap. tomo ii, orig. pp.1–8, scan n289–n294) is the expediente on the FEBRUARY 1778 rising of the gentiles of San Juan Capistrano, San Mateo, La Laguna and San Flores — it is the document behind Bancroft's 'Prov. St. Pap., MS., ii. 1-6' in the same footnote and is the immediate antecedent of the Pamó affair, but it concerns a different place and month, so linking it to this feature would be wrong. It would make a good standalone map feature.

features.name: Tenoqui Attack on Prospecting Soldiers
features.summary: Santa Bárbara backcountry. 2 soldiers killed, Spanish driven off.

sources.citation: Comte. Felipe de Goycoechea to Gov. Pedro Fages, Santa Bárbara, 2 Sept. 1790, narrative of the ambush of Sgt. Olivera's patrol at the ranchería de Tinoqui — Prov. St. Pap., Benicia Mil. (C-A 15), orig. pp.435–437 / Savage pp.209–211, scan n214–n216, Doc 296.

Felipe de Goycoechea, habilitado, 'Ajuste formalisado al Sold.o Gab.l Espinosa, que murió en veinte y nueve de Agosto de 1790', Santa Bárbara, 30 Aug. 1790 — Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 5), tomo ix, orig. p.324 / Savage p.180, scan n181, Doc 178.
sources.link_note: link probable, not confirmed by the record itself

sources.citation: Felipe de Goycoechea, habilitado, 'Ajuste formalisado al Sold.o Hilario Carlon, q.e murió en veinte y nueve de Agosto de 1790', Santa Bárbara, 29 Aug. 1790 — Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 5), tomo ix, orig. p.330 / Savage p.186, scan n187, Doc 184.
sources.link_note: link probable, not confirmed by the record itself

sources.citation: Comte. Felipe de Goycoechea to Gov. Pedro Fages, Santa Bárbara, 19 Oct. 1790, on the failure of the pursuit — Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 5), tomo ix, orig. pp.402–3 / Savage p.231, scan n232 (spans n232–n233), Doc 232.

Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, I:465–66 — 'In August 1790 Sergeant Olivera with eight men went in search of an Indian deserter, and were instructed also to prospect for mines... they were attacked by a large number of Indians of the Tenoqui rancheria and driven away with the loss of two soldiers killed, Espinosa and Carlon.'

features.notes: THE BEST-PAID-OFF FEATURE IN THIS BATCH: it was a bare 'Bancroft I.' and it now has the commanding officer's own narrative report plus the fiscal proof of both deaths. DATE REFINED: the map says 'August 1790'. The two soldiers' ajustes both close 'que murió en veinte y nueve de Agosto de 1790', so the engagement is 29 AUGUST 1790 (the patrol had set out 24 Aug. and the survivors did not regain Santa Bárbara until 1 Oct.). NAME DISCREPANCY, FLAGGED NOT RECONCILED: ca15-d296 as catalogued names the dead as 'Gabriel Espinosa & IGNACIO Carlón'; the habilitado's own ajuste and valúo (ca5-d184, ca5-d185) name him HILARIO Carlón, and Bancroft I:465 gives only the surname 'Carlon'. Hilario has the better authority — it appears twice, in accounting documents where the man's name governs a payment. RANCHERÍA SPELLING: Bancroft prints 'Tenoqui'; Goycoechea's report as catalogued reads 'Tinoqui'. The Napalayagua Indians (nine of them, enemies of Tinoqui) rode with the patrol. Bancroft adds that Goycoechea was blamed by Fages for risking his soldiers on mining work.

features.name: San Diego Uprising: Ranchería Participant List
features.summary: Full intelligence from C-A 15: 13+ rancherías identified. Gentile woman warned of second attack planned.

sources.citation: Tte. José Francisco de Ortega to Tte.-Col. Juan Bautista de Anza, informe on the San Diego revolt, San Diego, 30 Nov. 1775, ranchería roster at scan leaf n5 — Prov. St. Pap., Benicia Mil. (C-A 15), orig. pp.1–7 (roster at orig. p.5) / Savage pp.2–9, scan n2–n8, Doc 1.

Comandante Fernando de Rivera y Moncada and Sgt. Mariano Carrillo, expediente of Aug.–Sept. 1776 recording the confessions of the 1775 ringleaders and the ten rancherías invited into the plot — Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 1), tomo i. 221–232 / Savage pp.526–539, scan n223–n234, Doc 100.

Tte. José Francisco de Ortega, interrogation of 'el indio Carlos', capitán of the mission ranchería and principal ringleader, 11, 13 and 15 Apr. 1776 — Prov. St. Pap., Benicia Mil. (C-A 15), orig. pp.294–327 / Savage p.24, scan n23, Doc 27.
sources.link_note: link probable, not confirmed by the record itself

features.notes: The feature's date should probably read 1775 (event) / 30 Nov. 1775 (document). COUNT CHECK on '13+ rancherías': the leaf as catalogued names seven Christian rancherías (San Luis, Matamó[?], Tamacha[?], Meté, Yana, Abacaly[?] and the newly reduced San Miguel) and four named gentile ones (Melojó[?], Itai, Pocol, El Corral) plus '~6 more from the San Luis cañada' — so 11 named and roughly 17 in total, which supports '13+' but the map would be safer saying 'eleven named rancherías and about six more unnamed'. Bancroft's independent reading of the same leaf (I:253 n.28, 'Ortega in his Informe, MS., 5') gives the Christian list as San Luis, Matanió, Xanaali, Meti, Xana or Xanat, Abascal/Abuscal/Aguscal, and Magtate or San Miguel, and the gentile list as La Punta, Melejó... — i.e. Bancroft puts La Punta among the gentile rancherías, which the catalog's list does not. Two readings of one hand; worth a leaf check before the map states a definitive roster. THE 'GENTILE WOMAN' CLAIM IS NOT SUPPORTED BY WHAT I READ: the catalog summary of ca15-d1 attributes the warning of a second, planned dawn attack on the presidio within twenty days to the Christian Indian JOAQUÍN and the capitán MARIANO YGUATÍN[?] of the rancho de Aguacal[?] — both men. I found no gentile woman informant in this record. In ca1-d97 the informant is likewise a man, the californio Ignacio alias Diego. I am flagging this rather than reconciling it; the map's 'Gentile woman warned of second attack planned' needs a source or should be cut.

features.name: Battle at La Ciénega
features.summary: From hoja de servicios of Sargento Verdugo: under Capt. Rivera, "estuvieron el ataque que hicieron los gentiles en el parage de la Ciénega, en que se mataron 3."

sources.citation: Hoja de servicios of Sargento Mariano de la Luz Verdugo, aged 42, Monterey, 31 Dec. 1786 — Prov. St. Pap., Benicia Mil. (C-A 15), orig. p.335 / Savage pp.195–96, scan n200–n201, Doc 272.
Hoja de servicios of Sargento Mariano de la Luz Verdugo, 31 Dec. 1781 (signed Diego Gonzáles) — Prov. St. Pap., Benicia Mil. (C-A 15), orig. p.57 / Savage p.66, scan n67, Doc 82.

features.notes: I FETCHED AND READ THE LEAF ITSELF (C-A 15, scan n200, Savage stamp 195), and the map's quotation is wrong in three places. The manuscript reads: 'Campañas = "En toda la exped.n de San Diego y Monterey, y en el año de 1769 fué uno de los de la partida que de órden del Cap.n D.n Fernando de Rivera y Moncada SOSTUVIERON el ataque que hicieron los gentiles en el parage de la CIENEGUILLA en que se mataron 8; y en..."' Therefore: (1) the number killed is EIGHT, not three — the map's '3 killed' and its result field are wrong, and the catalog's '8 killed' is right; (2) the place is LA CIENEGUILLA, not La Ciénega — the feature name should change; (3) the verb is SOSTUVIERON ('they withstood/sustained'), not 'estuvieron', which also reverses the sense of the action: this was an attack MADE BY the gentiles which Rivera's party withstood, not a Spanish attack. The map's 'result: 3 killed' should become something like 'Spanish party withstands the attack; 8 killed'. Independent confirmation of 'Cieneguilla' comes from Verdugo's earlier 1781 service record (ca15-d82), which describes the same campaign as against 'the Cieneguilla gentiles'. CAUTION FOR THE MAP'S GEOGRAPHY: this is a 1769 action under Rivera y Moncada, whose 1769 march ran from Velicatá in Baja California to San Diego; a paraje called La Cieneguilla could lie on either side of the modern border. Nothing I read places it in Alta California, and I would not pin a coordinate without further evidence.

features.name: Toypurina's Revolt at San Gabriel
features.summary: MAJOR CONSPIRACY. Toypurina — female war leader of the Tongva (Gabrieleño) — organized multi-village uprising against Mission San Gabriel with neophyte alcalde Nicolás José. Plan to kill padres and soldiers. Betrayed by informant before attack could succeed. Toypurina and co-conspirators arrested. She was exiled to Mission San Carlos Borromeo. One of the most important indigenous military actors in California history.
features.result: Conspiracy foiled — Toypurina arrested and exiled

sources.citation: Gov. Pedro Fages to the Comandante General, San Gabriel, 30 Dec. 1785 (4 docs), with the continuation of 5 Jan. 1786 — Provincial Records (C-A 22), tomo ii, ff.131–133 (orig. pp.521–526, the San Gabriel entries at orig. pp.528–531) / Savage pp.348–351, scan n349–n351, Doc 2042.

Gov. Pedro Fages to Tte. José de Zúñiga, 22 Nov. 1785, ordering the Indian justicias of San Gabriel deposed, the ringleaders arrested and 15–20 lashes given to the rebellious — Provincial Records (C-A 23), tomo iii, orig. p.637 / Savage p.261, scan n262, Doc 685.
sources.link_note: link probable, not confirmed by the record itself

sources.citation: Gov. Pedro Fages to the Comandante General, Santa Bárbara / Monterey, 1786, on Sgt. Ignacio Olivera having punished two San Gabriel rebels without authority — Provincial Records (C-A 22), tomo ii, orig. pp.540–544 / Savage pp.352–355, scan n352–n355, Doc 2043.

Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, I:460 and n.21 — 'In October 1785 the neophytes and gentiles were tempted by a woman, so at least said the men, into a plan to attack the mission and kill the friars... Two years later came General Ugarte's order condemning one native, Nicolás, to six years of work at the presidio followed by exile to a distant mission. The woman was sent into perpetual exile.'
Rose Marie Beebe and Robert M. Senkewicz, Lands of Promise and Despair: Chronicles of Early California, 1535–1846, 247–49.
Comandante General Jacobo Ugarte y Loyola to Gov. Pedro Fages, 14 Dec. 1787, sentencing the conspirators — Archivo del Arzobispado / Archives of Santa Bárbara, MS., vi. 110–17.
Hugo Reid, letters on the Indians of Los Angeles County, Los Angeles Star, February–July 1852 (22 letters).

features.notes: MAJOR RESULT: this feature had no manuscript link at all, and there IS one. I fetched C-A 22 leaf n350 (Savage stamp 349, tomo folio 132) and read Savage's abstract of Fages's letter to the Comandante General from San Gabriel, 30 Dec. 1785: 'Que halló aquí presos á 7 Indios cristos. y 4 gentiles INCLUSA LA AUTORA DEL MOTÍN, y dos capitancillos gentiles ademas, á cuyos cabecillas se forma la corresp.te sumaria, sentenciando á los restantes á la pena de 15 á 20 azotes.' 'La autora del motín' — the female author of the rising — is Toypurina, named here only by her role. Immediately below, the entry of 5 Jan. 1786: 'Pasa las diligs. practicadas contra los cuatro Indios cabecillas del motín (de S. Gabl.) y que quedan castigados los 17 cómplices.' So the C-A record gives eleven prisoners held at San Gabriel (7 Christians, 4 gentiles), four ringleaders tried, 17 accomplices punished. NOTE THE ARITHMETIC TENSION with Bancroft I:460, who says the corporal 'captured some twenty of the conspirators' — 11 held at San Gabriel is not 20; the counts may cover different moments. Flagging, not reconciling. TWO FURTHER CHECKS I RAN AND REPORT NEGATIVE: (a) ca22-d2034 (Fages, 'Reflections on the Gabrieleño Indians' plan to kill padres & soldiers') looked like a candidate but is dated 10 Feb. 1784 — I pulled leaf n315 and the surrounding entries are all January–February 1784, so it PREDATES Toypurina by twenty months and I have not linked it. It may record a separate, earlier Gabrieleño conspiracy worth its own investigation. (b) I searched C-A 4 and C-A 23 for Ugarte's Dec. 1787 sentence (Nicolás José to six years' presidio labour and exile, Toypurina to perpetual exile) and found nothing; Bancroft cites it to Arch. Sta. Bárbara, MS., vi. 110-17, which is not a C-A document. The exile to Mission San Carlos Borromeo asserted in the map summary is not attested in anything I read here.

features.name: Yuma Revolt (Colorado River Massacre)
features.summary: DECISIVE YUMA VICTORY. 2 mission-pueblos (La Purísima Concepción, San Pedro y San Pablo) destroyed. 46+ dead including 4 Franciscan friars. Overland route from Sonora to California closed for 40+ years.
features.result: DECISIVE YUMA VICTORY — overland route closed

features.notes: This feature is exceptionally well covered in C-A and the existing citation ('C-A 22') pointed at the wrong volume for the best evidence: the eyewitness core is a series of SEVEN survivor depositions taken at Sonoyta on 31 October 1781 and copied into C-A 2, not C-A 22. Each deponent gets his own entry and link below, as instructed. CROSS-CHECKS AGAINST THE MAP TEXT: the date '17–18 July 1781' is confirmed by ca2-d170 ('the 17–18 July 1781 destruction'). The two mission-pueblos are named in the depositions as La Purísima Concepción and San Pedro y San Pablo de Bicuñer, matching the map. I did NOT find a manuscript confirming the map's '46+ dead including 4 Franciscan friars' — that figure comes from the printed literature (Arricivita, Bancroft) and should stay attributed there until someone reads the fuller depositions. CAUSATION: two rival explanations survive in the archive, and the map's summary offers none — ca22-d2024 (Neve) blames Spanish conduct (the captain taking gentile and Christian women at Jalchedún, Rivera's failure to gift the Yuma chief Palma, and the expedition's mules destroying the mesquite the Yumas live on part of the year), while ca2-d173 (the settler Matías de Castro) blames the cepo, Islas having jailed Ignacio Palma and the dead governor's son for trying to kill the soldier Cayetano Mesa. Worth surfacing on the map.

features.notes: THE EXISTING CITATION IS A MIS-MATCH AND I AM CORRECTING IT. 'C-A 22, n300, pp. 286–88. Neve to Com. Gral.' fuses two different records: leaf n300 of C-A 22 carries ca22-d320 (Neve, 16 May 1781, orig. pp.282–288 — so 'pp.286-88' fits THIS one) and the opening of ca22-d2029 (Savage pp.300–302), while the Savage page range 286–288 belongs to a THIRD record, ca22-d2024 (Neve's 'Antecedentes de una mortandad', scan n286–n288). Of the three, ca22-d320 is the one whose page range the citation actually matches and whose subject is genuinely Rivera — but note what it is: a pre-event dispatch order of 16 May 1781, two months BEFORE the killing. It does not attest the death. I have kept it, correctly described, and added the records that do. SECOND: the map says 'all 11–12 soldiers killed at separate camp on east bank.' The C-A records I read support the escort's size — ca22-d320 has 'Sgt Juan José Robles + 12 soldiers to the Colorado to meet Capt. Fernando Rivera' — but I found nothing in these records specifying the east bank or that all of them died, so those details should stay attributed to the printed literature. THIRD: the depositions give the manner of death (a flechazos, by arrows) and Croix's estate order fixes the month ('hasta Julio, día de su fallecimiento'), so 'July 1781' is archivally secure; 17–18 July comes from ca2-d170.

features.notes: THE MAP'S CITATION IS EXACTLY RIGHT AND I VERIFIED IT ON THE LEAF IMAGE — this is the cleanest existing link in the batch. Two small corrections to the feature's framing. (1) ADDRESSEE: the heading reads 'Fages á Neve', so this is Fages reporting to Governor Felipe de Neve, not to the Comandante General; the map does not state a recipient but the citation should. (2) GRAMMATICAL SUBJECT: Savage writes 'Que LLEGARON con felicidad al arruinado pueblo de la Purísima' — they arrived, i.e. the expedition, not Fages singly; and 'Que se comunicó con Romeu y Fueros', the two officers the map names. DATE: the feature is dated '1782' with year-confidence; the document is dated San Gabriel, 23 April 1782, so the date can be tightened. NOTE for accuracy: 'la Purísima' here is the Colorado River mission-pueblo of La Purísima Concepción (destroyed in the 1781 revolt), not Mission La Purísima Concepción in the Santa Bárbara Channel — an easy and consequential confusion on a California map, since one is on the Colorado and the other near Lompoc. The catalog summary of ca22-d287 omits the Romeu/Fueros clause that the leaf carries; that is a catalog-enrichment opportunity.

features.name: Ranchería Attack Near San José
features.summary: 6 leagues from San José. Multi-day pursuit. 15 volunteers + 18 soldiers. 11 killed, 31 captured.

sources.citation: Sgt. Luis Peralta, diary of the expedition against the gentiles, 19-27 Jan. 1805, dated San Francisco 30 Jan. 1805 - Provincial State Papers (BANC MSS C-A 12), tomo xix. 64-65 / scan n33-n34 (Savage pp. 33-34), Doc 24.

features.notes: The nearest C-A 11 records are Peralta's SEPTEMBER-OCTOBER 1804 raids in the same region under the same sergeant: ca11-d394 (29 Sep 1804, pursuit of gentile assassins in the Sierra de San Jose), ca11-d396 (27 Oct, instructions for the second pursuit), ca11-d402 (26 Oct, second expedition: 11 Christian fugitives recovered, 32 gandules brought in). Bancroft cites these at II:133 n.40 as 'Prov. St. Pap., MS., xviii. 351-2, 356' and calls them 'two unimportant raids'. They match the map's volume but NOT its numbers (nobody killed), so I have not linked them; if the map means the 1804 raids rather than the 1805 battle, those three are the records. NUMBERS: Bancroft says 11 killed / 30 captured; Peralta's own diary (leaf n34, which I read) gives 5 gandules killed, then 5 more plus a girl, 25 women and 11 Indians taken.

features.name: San Juan Bautista Wheat-Field Arson
features.summary: INDIGENOUS ECONOMIC WARFARE. Wheat crop burned. Moraga captured capitanejo from Santa Cruz (pursued 3 years). Signs of sublevación.

features.name: Amador's Failed Attack at San José
features.summary: "Salió nulo el proyecto de atacar los Gentiles." Failed military operation by Sargento Pedro Amador.

sources.citation: Jose Dario Argüello to Gov. Diego de Borica, San Francisco, 30 Sept. 1797, 'Sobre un proyecto de ataque' - Provincial State Papers (BANC MSS C-A 9), tomo xvi, 1a pag. 48 / scan n30, Doc 26.

features.notes: SUBSTANTIVE CORRECTION - the feature misreads the Spanish. I downloaded leaf n30 and transcribed Savage verbatim: '+ 1797 Set. 30 San Fran.co / Arguello a Borica sobre un proyecto de ataque. Dice salio nulo el proyecto de atacar los Gentiles a la Mis.n S.n Jose segun diligencias q.e practico el Sarg.to Amador. 1a pag. 48'. The subject of 'atacar' is 'los Gentiles' and the object is the mission: the GENTILES' plan to attack Mission San Jose came to nothing, as established by Amador's inquiry. There was no Spanish attack, hence no failed Spanish operation. Bancroft reads it the same way (I:556; I:712). Recommend retitling (e.g. 'San Jose attack scare disproved, 1797') and reclassifying the type: an alarm found baseless, not a raid.

features.name: Fugitive Neophytes: Sacalan & Cuchillones

features.name: Indian Killed at Monterey Presidio
features.summary: Indian Choychi grabbed musket at 2 AM, wounded guard Quesadas with bayonet. Soldiers entered; Marín struck him on head — died 1½ hours later "echando sangre con espuma por la boca."

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 9), tomo xvi, Savage pp. 796-820 / scan n217-n219, Doc 365. Sal to Borica, Monterey, 28 Feb. 1797, with witness depositions.

features.notes: Three corrections/flags. (1) The record is Sal's report of 28 Feb. 1797; it does not state the 2 a.m. hour the feature gives, so '2 AM' is unconfirmed from the catalog. (2) The feature treats 'guard Quesadas' and 'Marín' as two men; Savage names the wounded soldier 'Marín Quesadas' and the man who struck the blow 'soldier Marín' — ambiguous, possibly one person. Flagged, not reconciled. (3) For the 'result' field: surgeon Pablo Soler testified Choychi already had two fractured ribs when brought in from San Luis (injured at capture) and died more from the chest contusion than the head blow, which undercuts a flat 'killed resisting'. Bancroft vol. I has no mention of Choychi or Quesadas (grepped); episode appears unpublished, so no book source.

features.name: Murder of Christian Indian Toribio

features.name: Amador Expedition to el Colorado

features.notes: Two substantive corrections. (1) CITATION FORM: 'n218' is not a leaf; the document is at scan n123. The old citation lands a reader on an unrelated 1799 petition. (2) THE EVENT: the record does not describe an Amador expedition. It is Argüello's written order forbidding force in recruiting gentiles, with Amador's marginal endorsement reporting that 'el Mtro' (the missionary) went to el Colorado and the gentiles fled at sight of him for fear of baptism. Amador is the reporting officer, not the man who went; 'type: raid' likely needs revising. I could not determine what 'el Colorado' is; in the SF/San José jurisdiction it is most likely a local place name, not the Colorado River (ca24-d943 concerns the Río Colorado but in a Baja/Santa Catalina context). Left unresolved rather than guessed. Context, not linked: the April 1798 Mission San José war scare (ca10-d81, d89, d90).

features.name: False Alarm: Attack on SLO, SM, Concepción
features.summary: Rumored multi-mission attack proved false. Viceroy Azanza "queda impuesto de la falsedad de la noticia."

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 10), tomo xvii, orig. p. 487 / Savage p. 221 (folio 219), scan leaf n221, Doc 273. Azanza to Borica, México, 6 March 1799, 'Sobre tranquilidad de los indios'.
Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. i, 1542-1800 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), 548-49.

features.notes: CITATION CORRECTION: the existing text 'C-A 10, n240, p. 487' mixes two different documents. Original page 487 is right, but scan leaf n240 is NOT this document — I pulled the record that actually sits on leaf n240 (ca10-d310, Azanza to Borica, 3 Aug 1799, 'Sobre arrivo de embarcn. americana', orig. p.562, about the Anglo-American frigate Elisa and John Kendrick's supercargo) and it has nothing to do with the mission alarm. The correct leaf for p.487 is n221. DATING: the feature is dated '1799' with year confidence; the document is exactly dated 6 March 1799, and it is a viceregal ACKNOWLEDGEMENT from México, so the rumour itself circulated in California in 1798. Bancroft places the false alarm in his 1798 paragraph (Hist. Cal. i. 548-9): 'There was a false alarm of impending attack on San Miguel, San Luis, and Purisima by the Tulare and channel Indians.' I could NOT resolve Bancroft's underlying footnote (Prov. Rec., MS., iv. 285; v. 210; vi. 106-7, 100; ix. 9; Prov. St. Pap., MS., xvii. 97, 100, 106-7) to a document about THIS alarm: the Prov. St. Pap. xvii page-runs he cites map onto the April–June 1798 San José Bay-Area scare (ca10-d81 leaf n96, ca10-d89 leaf n100, ca10-d112 leaf n120), which is the other half of the same Bancroft footnote, not the SLO/San Miguel/Purísima rumour. So ca10-d273 is the only C-A record that demonstrably concerns this feature.

features.notes: ⚠ CATALOGUE ERROR FOUND AND PROVEN FROM THE LEAF IMAGE. I downloaded the BookReader JPEG of C-A 24 leaf n560 (item 168036074_80_6_2, scale 2) and read Savage's hand directly. The manuscript reads: heading 'Indios "Tulares"'; body: 'Dice qe no conviene de ningun modo mandar Neofitos ni tropa á los Tulares en solicitud del Indio huido Agustin, por ser muchissimos los Gentiles y esponerse á una pelea fuerte qe atrasaria demasiadamte la conquista espiritual. p. 753.' The published catalog record ca10... ca24-d1028 is wrong in FIVE places: (1) heading given as 'Indios fugitivos' — the leaf says 'Indios "Tulares"'; (2) 'á los Frailes' — the leaf says 'á los TULARES'; (3) 'los Indios huidos Aguini [gentiles]' — the leaf says 'del Indio huido AGUSTIN' (one named runaway, not a group); (4) 'una pérdida fuerte' — the leaf says 'una PELEA fuerte'; (5) 'desgraciadamte' — the leaf says 'demasiadamte'. The MAP FEATURE'S quotation is therefore correct and the catalog record needs amending. This should be fed back to the C-A database as a leaf-verified field correction. Savage page on this leaf is stamped 558 with hand folio 235.

features.notes: NULL RESULT, RECORDED HONESTLY: the Muñoz diary is not in the C-A corpus. I searched all 34,567 records for 'Pizcache', 'Sujoyucomu', 'Nupchenche', 'Taulamne' and 'Latelate' — ZERO hits on every one. I also ran content searches on the diary title and on 'Moraga expedición Tulares 1806'. Bancroft cites the diary as a standalone titled MS ('Munoz, Diario de la Expedicion hecha por Don Gabriel Moraga, Alferez de la Compania de San Francisco, á los Nuevos Descubrimientos del Tular, 1806, MS.'), which in his citation system means a separate item in his collection, not a folio of the Archives of California. What C-A DOES hold is the administrative paper trail of the expedition, which is emitted below as real clickable evidence. DATING: Bancroft's abstract of the diary puts the Pizcache interview on 13 October 1806, which fits the feature's 'October 1806'. The chief's testimony as Bancroft renders it: 'a band of soldiers like these came from across the sierra (from New Mexico) 20 years ago and killed many of the Indians.'

GEOGRAPHY NOTE: Muñoz's 'Río Guadalupe' is the STANISLAUS, not the Tuolumne. The map's placement of this feature in the 'Tuolumne River area' therefore conflicts with Bancroft's identification of the stream; flagged, not reconciled. The hostile demonstration is Bancroft's 'Oct. 5th, Hostile demonstrations of the Indians, whose fears could not be removed,' with the party camped back at the Rio Guadalupe.
