Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 12), tomo xix, orig. pp. 295-96 / Savage pp. 118-19, scan leaves n120-n121, Doc 108. Arrillaga, San Diego, 9 October 1806: the Moraga-Muñoz column assembled.
sources.link_note: link probable, not confirmed by the record itself

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. ii, 1801-1824 (1885), 52 n.16 (Muñoz diary, entry of 3 October 1806).

features.notes: UNRESOLVED for a C-A manuscript of the encounter. Searched the whole corpus for 'Taulamne' — zero hits. Same finding as reg-16/17. DATE: Bancroft's abstract of the diary puts this at 3 October 1806, '6 l. E. up the river to a rancheria of Taulamne or Tahualamne (Tuolumne?) situated on inaccessible rocks' — the river being the Guadalupe/Stanislaus, which is consistent with the map's Knights Ferry placement. Note the ethnonym problem Bancroft himself raises: he suspects the Merced of 29 September may actually be Bear Creek 'in order to locate Tahualamne on what is now Tuolumne River', i.e. the identification of this rancheria's stream is contested in the literature. Not reconciled here.

features.name: Skirmish at Apaglamenes/Tationes
features.summary: Near Grayson, Stanislaus County. 30 armed heathen on opposite bank, "painted, bedecked with feathers." 12 shots fired. One Indian hit. "Soldier Morales came into the skirmish with half his chin shaved."

sources.citation: Fr. José Viader, Diario ó Noticia del Viage que acabo de hacer por mandato del Sr Gobernador y Padre Presidente, con el objeto de buscar parages ó Sitios para fundar Misiones, Agosto 1810, MS. (Bancroft Library titled manuscript, with a second copy from the Archivo de la Misión de Santa Bárbara; NOT in the Archives of California series), entry for 22 August 1810.
Sherburne F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820,' University of California Anthropological Records 16:6 (1960), note 7 (Viader, August 1810).
[No Archives of California manuscript found for this engagement.]
Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. ii, 1801-1824 (1885), 56 and n.36 (Viader's August 1810 diary abstracted).

features.notes: ⚠ CITATION CORRECTION. The existing source reads 'Viader diary (Cook note 7). C-A 12.' The Viader diaries are NOT in C-A 12. I searched the whole corpus for 'Viader' (10 hits, all unrelated: mission rosters, a neophyte-wage receipt, a baptism case, Solá correspondence) and ran targeted searches for the August 1810 mission-site reconnaissance in C-A 12, 25 and 26 — no record of it exists. Bancroft cites the source as 'Viader, Diario ó Noticia del Viage que acabo de hacer por mandato del Sr Gobernador y Padre Presidente, con el objeto de buscar parages ó Sitios para fundar Misiones, Agosto 1810, MS.' — a titled standalone manuscript — and adds explicitly that 'Viader's original diary in my possession and that copied from the archives of Santa Bárbara do not exactly agree in some details', i.e. the two known copies are a Bancroft Library MS and a copy from the Santa Bárbara mission archive. Neither is Archives of California. DATING/GEOGRAPHY: Bancroft's abstract places Tationes and Apaglamenes on 22 August 1810, on the far bank of the San Joaquin, which fits the feature's 'August 1810' and the Grayson, Stanislaus County placement. Bancroft also notes 'Most of the names were those of the chiefs', a caution worth carrying on the map.

features.name: Dawn Assault at Pescadero/Cholvones
features.summary: Delta — Old River area. "Before dawn we assaulted a village." 15 San José Christians recovered, 18 heathen men captured, 51 women (released — "went away very happy"). 2 prisoners escaped.

sources.citation: Fr. José Viader, Diario de una Entrada al Río de San Joaquín, Octubre 1810, MS. (Bancroft Library titled manuscript, with a second copy from the Archivo de la Misión de Santa Bárbara; NOT in the Archives of California series), entries of 19-22 October 1810.
Sherburne F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820,' University of California Anthropological Records 16:6 (1960), note 12 (Viader, October 1810).
[No Archives of California manuscript found for this engagement.]
Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. ii, 1801-1824 (1885), 56-57 n.37 and 92.

features.notes: ⚠ CITATION CORRECTION, same as reg-19: 'Viader diary (Cook note 12). C-A 12' — the diary is Bancroft's 'Viader, Diario de una Entrada al Rio de San Joaquin, Octubre 1810, MS.', a standalone titled manuscript, not a C-A folio. Searched and not found (see reg-19 evidence). NUMBERS DISCREPANCY, FLAGGED NOT RECONCILED: the map says '15 San José Christians recovered, 18 heathen men captured, 51 women (released)'. Bancroft, summarising the same expedition at ii. 92, says 'sixteen Christian Indians were recovered and eighteen gentiles captured by a sudden attack on a rancheria, to say nothing of fifty women taken and set free — all without bloodshed.' 15 vs 16 Christians and 51 vs 50 women. The map's figures presumably come from Cook's text of the diary and Bancroft's from his own copy; Bancroft himself warns the two known copies of Viader disagree in details. Worth a footnote on the map rather than a silent choice. Bancroft's abstract also confirms 'Oct. 22d, Corporal Pico sent home with captives' — the link to reg-24's Pico.

features.name: Battle of Suisun
features.summary: MAJOR ENGAGEMENT. Alf. Moraga, 17 cavalry vs. ~120 Sespesuña/Suisun warriors. Crossed Carquines Strait by boat. Hard fight — 18 captured (released, expected to die). Survivors in 3 huts: 2 stormed, all killed; 3rd set on fire — "bravely preferred to perish in the flames." 4 Spanish wounded (23.5% rate) — highest in any Spanish victory. Royal Order from Spain praised "glorious action." Moraga promoted; Herrera + Soto made sergeants.
features.result: Spanish tactical victory — highest casualty rate of any Spanish victory

quote.es: Chief Malaca: "Es mejor morir libres que vivir como esclavos, despreciados por nuestro Puy."

sources.citation: Prov. Rec. (BANC MSS C-A 25), tomo ix, orig. pp. 367-71 [= Bancroft's ix. 122-3, hand folio] / Savage pp. 371-372, scan leaves n374-n375, Doc 686. Arrillaga to the Viceroy, 28 June 1810, 'Sobre encuentro y campaña con gentiles'.

Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 12), tomo xix, orig. pp. 1016-1019 / Savage p. 313 [Bancroft cites xix. 314], scan leaf n319, Doc 395. Viceroy Venegas to the Governor, México, 12 November 1811: transmits the royal order rewarding the action of 22 May 1810.

Prov. Rec. (BANC MSS C-A 26), tomo xi, orig. pp. 723-24 / Savage pp. 223-24 [= Bancroft's xi. 222-3], scan leaves n223-n224, Doc 831. Governor to the commandant [Estudillo], La Soledad, 26 June 1812: transmits the viceroy's note of 12 November 1811 on Moraga's 'gloriosa acción' of 22 May 1810.

Prov. Rec. (BANC MSS C-A 26), tomo xi, orig. p. 593 / Savage B-593, scan leaf n447, Doc 1218. Arrillaga to the Comandante de San Francisco, Monterey, 16 June 1812: the real decreto granting Moraga the grade of Teniente de Caballería (⚠ this entry dates the action 20 May, not 22 May).

Prov. Rec. (BANC MSS C-A 26), tomo xi, orig. pp. 363-66 / Savage B-363-366, scan leaf n432, Doc 1203. Arrillaga to the Comandante de San Francisco, Monterey, 5 May / 5 June 1810: among the register items, 'salida del Alférez Gabriel Moraga con 17 hombres a aprehender la ranchería de [Suymaya]'.
sources.link_note: link probable, not confirmed by the record itself

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. ii, 1801-1824 (1885), 91-92 and n.24.

Mariano Guadalupe Vallejo, Recuerdos Históricos y Personales tocantes á la Alta California, MS. (Bancroft Library dictation; Bancroft short-titles it 'Vallejo, Hist. Cal., MS.'), i. 151-55. NOT part of the Archives of California series.
Juan Bautista Alvarado, Historia de California, MS. (Bancroft Library dictation), i. 69-70. NOT part of the Archives of California series.

features.notes: THE PAGE-NUMBER PUZZLE, SOLVED. Bancroft's 'Prov. Rec., MS., ix. 122-3' does not match the C-A record's fields at first sight (ca25-d686 is catalogued at tomo IX pp. 367-71, Savage p. 371-372, scan n374). It resolves through Savage's DUAL foliation: a neighbouring record in the same run, ca25-d649, carries savage_page '365/116', giving an offset of 249 between the stamped number and the hand folio. 371-249 = 122 and 372-249 = 123. So Savage 371-372 IS hand folio 122-123, and Bancroft was citing the hand folio. The map's citation is right and the record is right; I record the arithmetic so nobody 'corrects' it later. DATE DISCREPANCY INSIDE C-A: ca26-d1218 dates the 'gloriosa acción' to 20 May 1810 while ca26-d831, ca12-d395, Bancroft and the royal order all say 22 May. The catalog record already flags this ('⚠ fecha 20 May, no 22'). Not reconciled. NAME DISCREPANCY: the promoted corporals are 'Herrera y Soto' in ca26-d831, ca12-d395 and Bancroft, but 'José Correa y Francisco Soto' in ca26-d1218. Also 'Ventura' vs 'Buenaventura' Zúñiga. SOURCE CAUTION Bancroft raises and the map should carry: Vallejo's account describes a fight in the same region by José Sánchez in 1817 against the Suisunes under chief Malaca, and Bancroft judges 'It is possible that the author has confounded two different battles'; Alvarado, Hist. Cal., MS., i. 69-70 dates the affair 1817, puts Gabriel Moraga in command, and says Solano was captured on that occasion. Using Vallejo for 1810 detail is therefore risky.

features.name: Tense Encounter with Tauquimenes
features.summary: Sacramento River branch, delta. Standoff; no combat.

sources.citation: Fr. Ramón Abella, Diario de un registro de los ríos grandes, 1811, MS. (Bancroft Library titled manuscript; a second copy was in Duflot de Mofras's hands. NOT in the Archives of California series), entries of 23-27 October 1811.
[No Archives of California manuscript found for this encounter.]
Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. ii, 1801-1824 (1885), 321-23 and n.3.

features.notes: BANCROFT'S FOOTNOTE CHASED, RESULT NEGATIVE. The episode is Bancroft, Hist. Cal. ii. 321-23, and his source is 'Abella, Diario de un registro de los rios grandes, 1811, MS.' — a standalone titled manuscript, of which Duflot de Mofras also says 'Le journal manuscrit de cette exploration intéressante est entre nos mains.' Not a C-A citation. SPELLING: Bancroft renders the ethnonym 'Tarquimenes', the map 'Tauquimenes'; grep of vol2 for 'tauquimen/taquimen' returns nothing, for 'Tarquimenes' the Abella note. Worth normalising on the map. EXPEDITION DETAIL from Bancroft: Fr. Ramón Abella with Fr. Buenaventura Fortuni, Sergeant [José] Sánchez apparently commanding, 68 persons in several boats, 15 October to 30 October 1811; they named Points San Pablo and San Pedro, made the first recorded navigation of the Sacramento, and named the numerous Indians on it 'Tarquimenes'. This is a 15-day trip, so the map's 'October 1811' is right. Bancroft notes the Suisunes 'showed more timidity than hostility', consistent with the map's 'standoff, no combat', and that 'Two leagues distant was where Moraga's famous battle took place' — a direct tie to reg-21.

features.name: Soto's Battle
features.summary: LARGEST PITCHED BATTLE IN COLONIAL CA. Sgt. Soto + 12 soldiers from SF (by boat) + 100 Mission San José auxiliaries vs. ~1,000 warriors from 4 united rancherías (Unsumnes). Warriors pre-positioned on marshy island, women/children removed. "Fell upon the soldiers at landing." 3-hour battle. Soto "was at one time doubtful of the result, so reliant were the foes on their numbers, so careless of life." 1 neophyte killed (Alcalde Julio); many indigenous dead. Not a single fugitive captured.
features.result: Spanish tactical / INDIGENOUS STRATEGIC VICTORY — largest single-engagement indigenous army in CA

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 12), tomo xix, orig. pp. 1153-69 / Savage pp. 344-348, scan leaves n351-n355, Doc 425. Luis Argüello to Gov. Arrillaga, San Francisco, 31 October 1813, 'Expedición militar — Combate con los indios' (embodying Sgt. Francisco Soto's own narrative).
Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. ii, 1801-1824 (1885), 324 and n.4.
San José, Libro de Misión, MS., 25 (mission register, Mission San José). NOT in the Archives of California series.
Sgt. Francisco Soto, Expedición Militar del Sargento, 1813, MS. — Soto's own narrative, surviving embodied in Argüello's report (see the C-A entry above), not as a separately catalogued C-A document.
Sherburne F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820,' University of California Anthropological Records 16:6 (1960), 265-77.

features.notes: BEST RESULT IN THE BATCH. Bancroft's footnote says of Soto's narrative that 'The narrative is embodied in a report by Argüello' — and that report survives in C-A as ca12-d425, a five-leaf abstract. The map's Savage page range should be corrected from 334-348 to 344-348 (the record spans Savage 344-348, orig. pp. 1153-69, scan leaves n351-n355). DATE: the record dates the report 31 October 1813 and the battle at dawn on the 27th, matching the map's 27 October 1813. The San José mission book puts the departure against the Unsumnes on 25 October and names the killed alcalde Julio, which the C-A record independently confirms ('one auxiliary, Julio, killed'). The C-A abstract adds a detail not in Bancroft and worth putting on the map: the Indians had taunted that 'soldiers are worth nothing on foot, only on horseback', then learned otherwise; and Soto praises the auxiliaries' obedience and valour.

features.name: Pico's Fight at San Joaquin Crossing
features.summary: San Joaquin River between Dos Palos and Los Banos. Day 9: armed heathen crossing river, Cpl. Juarez engaged — killed 2. Day 10: Indians came to attack camp at dawn. Line of battle formed. Interpreter asked what they wanted — "to fight." After firing, troops dismounted and pursued through brush. 3 killed, 1 captured. Dead included a Christian from Santa Cruz who was "the one most determined" to kill the soldiers.

sources.citation: [Sgt. José Dolores] Pico, diary of the 1815 expedition to the San Joaquin, MS. — printed in Cook. Provenance NOT established as Archives of California; see notes.
[No Archives of California manuscript found for this engagement.]
Sherburne F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820,' University of California Anthropological Records 16:6 (1960), 271-74 (Pico diary, November 1815).

Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. ii, 1801-1824 (1885), 326 and n.7 (the 1815 'gran expedición': Solá's letters 14 Sept - 9 Nov; Moraga's northern party of 50 against the Pitemas; Sgt. Pico bringing in 11 Indians, Solá to Ruiz, 5 Oct 1815).

features.notes: ⚠ CITATION PROBLEM AND AN OPEN HISTORIOGRAPHICAL CONFLICT. (1) C-A 13 cannot hold this: q.py vol 13 shows it is Prov. St. Pap. tomo XX, whose records run 1816-1821; the 1815 material is not there. C-A 12 (tomo XIX) I searched directly and found nothing. (2) Bancroft, Hist. Cal. ii. 326, says flatly of the 1815 gran expedición: 'It is only from allusions in the archives that this affair is known, for no diary is extant.' Cook nevertheless prints a Pico diary at pp. 271-74. Either the diary surfaced after Bancroft wrote, or Cook used a copy Bancroft did not connect to this campaign. I cannot resolve that from here and will not guess. (3) Bancroft's own manuscript pointers for the 1815 campaign are 'Prov. St. Pap., Ben. Mil., MS., xlvi. 32-4' (the northern party of 50 under Gabriel Moraga against the Pitemas, out from San Francisco about 25 Sept) and 'Sola to Ruiz, Oct. 5, 1815. Id., xlvi. 5-6' (Sgt. Pico bringing in 11 Indians charged with killing Christians and wounding vaqueros). Prov. St. Pap. Benicia Military is C-A 17, but Savage's abstracts in that stretch carry NO original page numbers (the orig_page field is empty throughout), so the page-interval resolver cannot reach them, and my content searches of C-A 17 for a 1815 Pico entry found nothing. This is a genuine gap, not a search failure I can close. (4) DATE: the map's 'November 9-10, 1815' is consistent with Bancroft's note that Solá's letters on this expedition run 'Sept. 14th to Nov. 9th' and that the expedition returned 1 December 1815 (Tapis to Guerra, 2 Dec).

features.name: Ortega's Raid on Tache
features.summary: Tache village, Kings River, not far west of Lemoore (Cook note [2]). Ortega attacked at dawn but village deserted — fugitive Indians had warned them "the soldiers were coming to kill them at the point of the lance." Found 3 Soledad horses. Followed into tule swamp but could not reach inhabitants.

sources.citation: Sherburne F. Cook, "Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800–1820," University of California Anthropological Records 16:6 (Berkeley, 1960), 267–69 (Ortega's diary, in translation); Cook note [2] places Tachi territory west of Tulare Lake, villages near Lemoore.

Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. II (San Francisco, 1885), 326 and 326 n.8 — Solá's 'grand expedition' of autumn 1815 in pursuit of runaways; 'Diego Olivera was one of the party from Santa Barbara, under Juan Ortega … which met another from Monterey over in the Tulares'; the expedition had returned by 1 Dec. 1815 (Tapis to Guerra, 2 Dec. 1815).

Gob. Pablo Vicente de Solá to Sgt. Juan de Ortega, Monterey, 1 Nov. 1815 — the operational order for this raid: Provincial Records (C-A 26), tomo xi, orig. pp. 98–100 / Savage p. 28, scan n27, Doc 93.
sources.link_note: link probable, not confirmed by the record itself

features.notes: LEAF-VERIFIED FIELD CORRECTION: I downloaded C-A 26 scan n27 (BookReader JPEG) and read Savage's entry verbatim. It reads: 'A Sargto Juan de Ortega. / Nove 1o. — 2o con partida de Presidio de Sta Barba y 15 hombres mas hará una expedicion del 6 al 11, pr los parajes inmediatos en persecucion de gentiles: qe el Sargto Jose Dolores Pico se le unirá y entonces hará correrias pr Misiones de Sn Miguel, Sn Antº Soledad y otras, con ambas partidas. pp. 98-100.' The catalog summary for ca26-d93 says 'Con 18 hombres del Presidio de Sta Bárbara'; the leaf says the SB presidio party PLUS 15 more men ('y 15 hombres mas'). That is a catalog error worth correcting. NULL RESULT (record it): the Ortega diary Cook translated is NOT in the Archives of California so far as I can find. I grepped the whole 34,567-record catalog for Tach/Tache/Tachi (word-boundary, case-sensitive) and for diario/expedicion/tular restricted to 1815 — zero diary hits. Bancroft II:326 states outright of this expedition that 'no diary is extant,' which is consistent: Cook's text must come from a repository outside C-A, and I could not establish which one. Do not fabricate a C-A link for the diary itself.

features.name: Pico's Raid on Cheneche
features.summary: Cheneche village near mouth of Mariposa Creek, north of Los Banos, on the San Joaquin River. Pre-dawn assault at 4 AM. 66 captured (Christians and heathen). Released 4 men and 12 crippled old women. "Majority of the people escaped because this village is in a bad location." Found 7 live horses and 5 recently dead.
features.result: Mostly escaped — bad terrain for pursuit

sources.citation: Sherburne F. Cook, "Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800–1820," University of California Anthropological Records 16:6 (Berkeley, 1960), 270–71 (Pico's diary, in translation); Cook note [9] places the Cheneches near the mouth of Mariposa Creek.

Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. II (San Francisco, 1885), 326 and 326 n.8 — Solá's grand expedition of 1815; the Monterey party met the Santa Bárbara party in the Tulares; in the south 'Sergt. Pico brought in 11 Indians charged with killing Christians and wounding vaqueros' (Solá to Ruiz, 5 Oct. 1815, Prov. St. Pap., Ben. Mil., MS., xlvi. 5-6).

Gob. Pablo Vicente de Solá to Sgt. Juan de Ortega, Monterey, 1 Nov. 1815, ordering Sgt. José Dolores Pico to join him: Provincial Records (C-A 26), tomo xi, orig. pp. 98–100 / Savage p. 28, scan n27, Doc 93.
sources.link_note: link probable, not confirmed by the record itself

features.notes: Same expedition as reg-25, opposite wing. Pico commanded the Monterey party; Ortega the Santa Bárbara party; Bancroft says the two met in the Tulares. The 8 November date for Cheneche falls inside the '6 al 11' window of the order. NULL RESULT: no Pico 1815 diary exists anywhere in the C-A catalog (word-boundary greps for Cheneche, Malim, Tape/Tapee, Nupchenche across all 34,567 records returned nothing; Bancroft II:326 says no diary of this expedition is extant). Cook's source repository is not established.

features.name: Tapee Horse Slaughter
features.summary: Village of Tapee (Tape), south of the great bend of the San Joaquin River, ~20 miles west of Fresno (Cook note [9]). Pico surrounded village on both sides of river. Found 238 RECENTLY KILLED ANIMALS, "a great deal of meat quartered and dried," and 16 live animals shot with arrows or badly treated. "From Tapee to Cheneches... more than 500 dead animals." LARGEST INDIGENOUS ECONOMIC WARFARE INCIDENT.
features.result: INDIGENOUS ECONOMIC WARFARE — 238+ horses killed, 500+ in region

sources.citation: Sherburne F. Cook, "Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800–1820," University of California Anthropological Records 16:6 (Berkeley, 1960), 275–76 (Pico's diary, in translation); Cook note [9] places Tape ~20 mi. west of Fresno, south of the great bend of the San Joaquin.
Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. II (San Francisco, 1885), 326 and 326 n.8 — the 1815 grand expedition, its two parties, and its return on 1 December 1815.

Gob. Pablo Vicente de Solá to Sgt. Juan de Ortega, Monterey, 1 Nov. 1815, ordering the joint correrías by the missions of San Miguel, San Antonio and Soledad 'con ambas partidas': Provincial Records (C-A 26), tomo xi, orig. pp. 98–100 / Savage p. 28, scan n27, Doc 93.
sources.link_note: link probable, not confirmed by the record itself

features.notes: The 23 November date falls AFTER the 6–11 November window of the order, in its second phase: 'el Sargto Jose Dolores Pico se le unirá y entonces hará correrias pr Misiones de Sn Miguel, Sn Antº Soledad y otras, con ambas partidas' (verbatim from scan n27). Tapee, ~20 mi west of Fresno, lies in exactly the interior hinterland reached from San Miguel/Soledad, and Bancroft II:326 n.8 records the whole expedition returning 1 December 1815 — so a 23 November action is chronologically inside it. NULL RESULT: no C-A record mentions Tape/Tapee, and no C-A record anywhere reports the 238 slaughtered horses. That figure survives only in Cook's translation of the Pico diary. Given its importance to the feature ('largest indigenous economic warfare incident'), the absence of any archival corroboration in C-A should be stated on the map rather than papered over.

features.name: Search for Malim Village
features.summary: Junction of Mariposa Creek and the San Joaquin River, near Los Banos. Guide (from Malim village) told them he knew the way, then when they arrived said he didn't know where it was — "but he did know that this was his country and we were hunting for his village." Guide given 10 lashes. Village found but inhabitants had escaped. 2 Christians from Santa Cruz captured.

sources.citation: Sherburne F. Cook, "Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800–1820," University of California Anthropological Records 16:6 (Berkeley, 1960), 277–78 (Pico's diary, in translation); Cook note [9] places Malim between the Cheneches and the Nupchenches along the San Joaquin River.
Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. II (San Francisco, 1885), 326 and 326 n.8 — the 1815 grand expedition and its return on 1 December 1815.

Gob. Pablo Vicente de Solá to Sgt. Juan de Ortega, Monterey, 1 Nov. 1815, ordering the joint correrías by the missions of San Miguel, San Antonio and Soledad 'con ambas partidas': Provincial Records (C-A 26), tomo xi, orig. pp. 98–100 / Savage p. 28, scan n27, Doc 93.
sources.link_note: link probable, not confirmed by the record itself

features.notes: 27–28 November falls in the second phase of the order (the joint correrías 'con ambas partidas'), inside the expedition's chronology (home 1 Dec. 1815 per Bancroft II:326 n.8). NULL RESULT: the catalog has no record mentioning Malim; the only C-A occurrences of anything like the name are 'Malmi' near Santa Cruz (ca13-d110/d111, June 1816) — a completely different place and event, and it should NOT be linked here. The Pico diary itself is not in C-A.

features.name: Martinez Incident at Bubal
features.summary: Village of Bubal (Wowol), western shore of Tulare Lake (Cook note [6]). Fr. Luis Antonio Martinez burned village of Pusas. Lively controversy with other friars over his behavior.

sources.citation: Sherburne F. Cook, "Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800–1820," University of California Anthropological Records 16:6 (Berkeley, 1960), 279–86 (Padre Luis Antonio Martínez's tular entrada, in translation); Cook note [6] identifies Bubal as Wowol on the shore of Tulare Lake.

Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. II (San Francisco, 1885), 327–28 and 327 n.11 — 'Padre Luis Martinez visited these rancherias early in 1816'; the party left San Luis Obispo and visited Lucluc (28 lgs.), Tuohuala (9 l.), Gelecto (18 l.), Lihuanhilame (19 l.), Quihuame (7 l.); Telame mentioned but not visited; 'Tuohuala was called also Hubal (Bubal?).' Bancroft then narrates the ensuing quarrel among the friars over the soldiers' conduct.
Martínez, "Entrada á las Rancherías del Tular, 1816," MS — the diary itself, cited by Bancroft under his own manuscript title (Hist. Cal. II:327 n.11).

Cabot to the prefect, and Sarría to the governor, 1 June 1816: Archivo del Arzobispado [de San Francisco], MS, iii. pt. i. 46–49, 51–53, 119–20 — the inter-Franciscan controversy over the soldiers' conduct on this entrada (Bancroft, Hist. Cal. II:328 n.12).

features.notes: NULL RESULT, recorded honestly: there is NO Archives of California record of this entrada. What I tried: (1) word-boundary greps over all 34,567 records for Bubal, Pusas, Tach*, and the other ranchería names — nothing; (2) a full listing of every C-A record dated April–July 1816 (about 90 records, read) — nothing on a tular entrada; (3) year-scoped content searches on tular/expedición/ranchería/gentil for 1816 — the only hits are the Moraga/Malmi affair near Santa Cruz and routine cimarrón orders. The nearest thing is ca26-d1127 (Solá borrador, 11 June 1816, 'instruido de lo ocurrido en la expedición'), which is too vague to attach — it could equally be the Malmi raid — so I am not linking it. DATE FLAG: the feature dates this May 1816; Bancroft says Padre Luis Martínez 'visited these rancherias early in 1816.' A May date is compatible with the friars' controversy correspondence of 1 June 1816 but Bancroft does not state a month. Do not silently harmonise. NAME FLAG: Bancroft's itinerary gives 'Tuohuala … called also Hubal (Bubal?)' — the identification of Bubal with Wowol on Tulare Lake is Cook's, not the manuscript's.

features.name: Battle at Malime/Tasnil
features.summary: Near Santa Cruz. Inter-indigenous: Christians vs. gentiles. 4 killed.

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. II (San Francisco, 1885), 328 n.14 ('June, 1816, Moraga made a fruitless expedition against apostate Christians at Malmi rancheria near Santa Cruz. Prov. St. Pap., MS., xx. 103') and II:390 (Santa Cruz annals: the rancherías of Pitemas and of Malmi named for 1815–16).

Luis Argüello to the Gov. of Alta California, San Francisco, 21 June 1816 — Alf. Gabriel Moraga setting out in force against the apostate Indians at the ranchería/pueblo of 'Malmi' in the Santa Cruz mission jurisdiction: Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 13), tomo xx, orig. pp. 386–88 / Savage p. 104, scan n103, Doc 110.

Luis Argüello to Gob. Solá, San Francisco, 30 June 1816 — the surprise on the apostate Christians of Malmi failed, they were no longer there: Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 13), tomo xx, orig. pp. 389–91 / Savage pp. 104–105, scan n103–n104, Doc 111.

features.notes: SERIOUS DISCREPANCY — do not reconcile silently. The feature says December 1816, inter-indigenous (Christians vs. gentiles), 4 killed. The only documented Malmi engagement is Gabriel Moraga's expedition of June 1816, which was a Spanish military operation, not inter-indigenous, and which FAILED because the apostates had already left — no one was killed. I listed every C-A record dated Nov 1816 – Feb 1817 (about 80 records, read) and there is no December 1816 action near Santa Cruz at all. 'Tasnil' appears nowhere: not in the 34,567-record catalog, not in Bancroft's History of California vol. II. Bancroft II:390 says only that in 1815–16 'there had been expeditions after runaway neophytes of which not much is known, but the rancherias of Pitemas and of Malmi are named.' Recommendation: either re-date this feature to June 1816 and re-describe it as a failed Spanish surprise, or mark the December 1816 / 4-killed / inter-indigenous details as unsourced. The two C-A records below are offered as the correct records for the Malmi episode, NOT as confirmation of the feature as currently written.

features.name: Armed Encounter on Sacramento
features.summary: Sacramento River, ~50 miles from SF. Standoff; Spanish retreated.

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. II (San Francisco, 1885), 331 and 331 n.37, citing Argüello (Luis), Hoja de Servicios, 1828, MS — a seventeen-day voyage up the Sacramento 'constantly threatened by the numerous Indians, and once landing with four men to fight them.'

Hoja de servicio of Capt. Luis Antonio Argüello, certified by Ignacio Martínez, San Francisco, 31 Dec. 1828 — records his expedition up the river debouching at San Francisco (10 men, 17 days, attacked): State Papers, Sacramento (C-A 56), tomo xi, orig. to p. 90 / Savage pp. 120–22, scan n119–n121, Doc 138.

features.notes: CITATION PROBLEM. I checked every occurrence of '1817' in Bancroft's Indian-affairs / explorations chapter of vol. II (the whole span from the chapter head through the notes on Indian affairs of the decade) and there is no May 1817 armed encounter on the Sacramento in Bancroft II. The bare citation 'Bancroft II.' cannot be verified as written. The closest Bancroft passage is II:331 with its note 37, resting on Luis Argüello's Hoja de Servicios: 'in this same month of May he went to explore the river that flows from the north into San Francisco Bay, that is the Sacramento, sailing on it for seventeen days, constantly threatened by the numerous Indians, and once landing with four men to fight them,' which Bancroft assigns to May 1818 but then argues 'was probably made one or two years earlier.' DATE CONFLICT, unreconciled: the hoja as catalogued in C-A reads 1808; Bancroft read May 1818; Bancroft's own guess is 1816–17; the map says May 1817. Four different dates for what may be one voyage. RESEARCH LEAD, not a claim: the May 1817 Sacramento voyage of Luis Argüello with Padres Narciso Durán and Ramón Abella is documented by Durán's own diary, which is not in C-A; if that is the map compiler's real source, the citation should be changed from 'Bancroft II.' to Durán's diary. I did not verify this and am not asserting it.

features.name: Skirmish with Fugitives on Sacramento
features.summary: Sacramento delta island. Minor skirmish; 1 wounded.

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. II (San Francisco, 1885) — citation as given on the feature; the specific engagement could not be located in this volume.

features.notes: UNRESOLVED, recorded as a finding. What I tried: (1) grepped every '1817' occurrence in Bancroft II's explorations-and-Indian-affairs chapter — no May 1817 Sacramento skirmish exists there, so the feature's 'Bancroft II.' citation cannot be substantiated; (2) listed every C-A record dated April–July 1817 (about 40 records, read in full) — nothing on a river expedition; (3) year-scoped content searches on Sacramento / San Joaquín / lancha / expedición for 1817 — nothing. The one C-A item close in kind, ca26-d161 (Solá, 10 June 1817, 'El Sargto. distinguido Juan Ortega no pudo coger a los indios fugitivos'), gives no location and I am deliberately NOT linking it. I also considered ca56-d138 (Luis Argüello's hoja, the 17-day Sacramento voyage under attack, linked on reg-31) but the feature's two distinguishing details — a delta island and one man wounded — appear nowhere in that record, and attaching it here would be exactly the kind of plausible-looking wrong link that is worse than a gap. RESEARCH LEAD, not a claim: the Argüello–Durán voyage of May 1817 is documented by Fray Narciso Durán's diary, which is outside the C-A series; if that is the compiler's real source the citation needs changing. Unverified.

features.name: Campaign against Muquelenis
features.summary: Mokelumne, eastern delta. Spanish reported success.

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. II (San Francisco, 1885), 335 and 335 nn. 31–32 — 'Victory of Sanchez over the Moquelumnes'; 27 pagans killed, 20 wounded, 16 captured, 49 horses taken; Padre Durán names the offending gentiles Muquelemes.

Solá's borradores, pt. 4 (artillery and campaigns), San Juan Bautista / Rancho del Rey / Monterey, Jul.–Dec. 1819 — the successful campaign against the Ranchería de los Muquelemnes reported to the Viceroy, Padre Narciso Durán named: State Papers, Sacramento (C-A 54), tomo i, Savage pp. 239–46, scan n238–n245, Doc 154.

Gob. Solá to Tte. Gabriel Moraga, San Carlos, 24 Sept. 1819 — the instruction forming the multi-pronged 1819 campaign, including 'a SF party of 20–25 under Sgt. Sánchez via San José, and a launch with a cannon by water': Prov. St. Pap., Benicia Mil. (C-A 17), orig. pp. 421–22 / Savage pp. 228–29, scan n227–n228, Doc 284.

Gob. Solá to de la Guerra, 7 Oct. 1819, 'Campaña contra indios' — approving that each presidio mount its own expedition within its own demarcation: Prov. St. Pap., Benicia Mil. (C-A 17), orig. pp. 425–30 / Savage pp. 232–33, scan n231–n232, Doc 288.
sources.link_note: link probable, not confirmed by the record itself

sources.citation: Gob. Solá to de la Guerra (in México), Monterey, 6 Jan. 1820 — the 1819 expeditions had poor results, but Sgt. Sánchez's was 'muy brillante'; recommends him for the grade of alférez: Prov. St. Pap., Benicia Mil. (C-A 17), orig. p. 455 / Savage p. 241, scan n240, Doc 300.
sources.link_note: link probable, not confirmed by the record itself

sources.citation: Padre Narciso Durán to Solá, 2 June and 28 Oct. 1819: Archivo del Arzobispado [de San Francisco], MS, iii. pt. ii. 82–84, 104–105 — the letters in which the offending gentiles are named 'Muquelemes' (Bancroft, Hist. Cal. II:335 n.32).
Amador, "Memorias," MS, 15–16 — the eyewitness account of José María Amador, one of the five soldiers wounded in the fight (Bancroft, Hist. Cal. II:335 and n.32).

features.notes: Strongest C-A result in this batch. Bancroft II:335 supplies the detail the feature compresses to 'Spanish reported success': Sgt. José Sánchez marched from San Francisco by way of San José in early October 1819 with 25 men, fought in the region of modern Stockton, killed 27, wounded 20, captured 16 and took 49 horses, losing one neophyte ally with five soldiers wounded (one of them José María Amador); the force was back before the end of October and Sánchez was recommended for promotion. Padre Durán's naming of the offenders as 'Muquelemes' is, Bancroft notes, perhaps the first writing of the name. ONE DISCREPANCY, flagged not reconciled: Savage's abstract of ca17-d300 describes Sánchez's expedition as being in the Santa Cruz direction, whereas Bancroft places the fight in the lower San Joaquin near Stockton. The leaf has not been re-read to settle whether that is Savage's error, Solá's, or a second expedition. Also noted: the catalog summary of ca54-d154 itself carries an internal cross-reference '= mil-history register #33', so that one record is not fully independent of the register being annotated; I have therefore rested the verification on the Bancroft correspondence and on ca17-d284, which are independent.

features.name: Garcia's Battle at Jayaya/Tape
features.summary: Beyond Santa Rita, near SJB. Spanish nearly defeated; chaotic retreat.

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. II (San Francisco, 1885), 338–39, note 38 — the fight at the rancherías of Jayaya and Tape beyond Santa Rita, from Garcia, Hechos, MS., 10–15.
García (Inocente), "Hechos Históricos de California," MS, 10–15 — the participant's own dictated narrative, the sole source for this engagement.

features.notes: UNRESOLVED for C-A, and the reason matters. Bancroft prints this episode inside his closing note on Californio personal narratives, where he says explicitly that such items are 'statements more or less inaccurate but founded on facts not clearly recorded in the archives, which it would be hazardous to embody in chronological history.' In other words, Bancroft himself found no archival record of it. My own search agrees: word-boundary greps across all 34,567 C-A records for Jayay* and Tape/Tapee return nothing, and a search for Inocente García in the period returns only his later career (Rancho Natividad 1827, administrator of Mission San Miguel 1839–40). Bancroft's version supplies detail the feature omits and should be carried on the map: six men including Inocente García, under Sgt. José Dolores Pico, went with Padre Felipe Arroyo de la Cuesta and 30 Indian auxiliaries from San Juan Bautista beyond Santa Rita to the rancherías of Jayaya and Tape to collect girls promised as converts; the chief was absent, a fight followed, most of the party ran, García and a few continued against the sergeant's orders and rescued all but two who were killed, along with all the horses; Pico put García in the stocks and the governor pardoned him at Arroyo's intercession. DATE FLAG: Bancroft gives no year for this item; the feature's 'ca. 1815–20' is an editorial estimate, not a source statement.

features.name: Boronda's Campaign at Tachi
features.summary: Tachi village, west of Tulare Lake near Lemoore (Cook note [2]: "not far west of Lemoore"). Same village Ortega raided in Nov 1815. "Arrows raining; underground defenses." Indigenous fortification.

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. II (San Francisco, 1885), 338–39, note 38 — '1812, etc., the Indians of Tachi had pits from which they discharged their arrows, into which the soldiers' horses often fell. Boronda, Notas, 15'; and '1813, Boronda gives some details of an expedition to Tachi in the Tulares region under Sergt. Espinoza. Notas, MS., 13–15.'

Boronda (José Canuto), "Notas Históricas sobre California," MS, 13–15 (the Tachi expedition under Sgt. Espinoza) and 15 (the arrow pits); cf. p. 2 (the river Reyes and Tache Lake, in connection with the 1815 grand expedition, which Boronda accompanied as a soldier).

features.notes: UNRESOLVED for C-A, plus a possible duplication problem worth the compiler's attention. (1) DATE CONFLICT: the feature dates this ca. 1815–20; Bancroft dates Boronda's Tachi expedition to 1813, under Sgt. Espinoza, and dates the arrow-pits detail to '1812, etc.' Neither is 1815–20. (2) POSSIBLE DUPLICATE OF reg-25: Bancroft also notes that 'Boronda, Notas, MS., 2, mentions the river Reyes and Tache Lake in connection with what seems to be this expedition' — meaning Solá's grand expedition of November 1815, which Boronda accompanied as a soldier. That is precisely the expedition in which Ortega raided Tache on 10 November 1815 (reg-25). So part of the Boronda Tachi material may be a second, dictation-based telling of reg-25 rather than a separate engagement, and the map may be double-counting. I am flagging this, not asserting it. (3) C-A search: word-boundary greps of all 34,567 records for Tach/Tache/Tachi return nothing; a search for an Espinosa expedition returns only ca12-d297 (Sgt. Miguel Espinosa, 13 Oct. 1809, San Antonio, a 20-day reconnaissance of a ranchería) which is four years early and unnamed as to place — I am deliberately NOT linking it. I also considered attaching ca26-d93 (the November 1815 order, linked on reg-25) but Bancroft's dating of the Boronda Tachi expedition to 1813 under Espinoza argues against it, so no link is offered.

features.name: Moraga's Failed Expedition to Amajava
features.summary: Interior Santa Barbara. "Impassable roads, no water/pasture. Sin haber podido llegar á la ranchería de los Amajavas." Gentiles attacked others as reprisal for mission punishment.

sources.citation: Gabriel Moraga to Gob. Solá, in the field, 16 Dec. 1819 — his own report of the expedition against the Amajava: set out with 50 men and 10 vecinos eastward, reached Mongarayait/Agallaga (the last pasture, 27 horses lost), carried water in vessels and went on inland; on the way back a gentile Indian killed one of his boys to rob him of his horse and blanket: Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 13), tomo xx, orig. pp. 1077–81 / Savage p. 239, scan n238–n239, Doc 304.

Gob. Solá to Tte. Narciso Fabregat, Monterey, 21 Dec. 1819 — the Mojave expedition failed to reach the Amajaba ranchería 'por la absoluta imposibilidad en que se hallan esos caminos, pastos, y agua para la caballada'; Fabregat and Moraga returned to Santa Bárbara 14 Dec.: Prov. St. Pap., Benicia Mil. (C-A 17), orig. p. 453 / Savage p. 241, scan n240, Doc 299.

Gob. Solá to Tte. Gabriel Moraga, Monterey, 3 Nov. 1819 — the final order for the Amajaba campaign: 50 men (35 cavalry from both presidios plus 15 Mazatlán infantry under Fabregat), the armament brought by Tte. Francisco Mª Ruiz, 4 artillerymen and a cannon with grape and ball; march at once to the Mojave ranchería, make the capitanejos surrender the fugitive Christians, then garrison San Gabriel and San Fernando with 15 men each: Prov. St. Pap., Benicia Mil. (C-A 17), orig. pp. 442–43 / Savage pp. 236–38, scan n235–n237, Doc 296.

Gob. Solá to Tte. Gabriel Moraga, San Carlos, 24 Sept. 1819 — the instruction forming the 1819 campaign against the 'indios prófugos,' 'deseoso de dar una castigada general á los gentiles por… abrigar en sus rancherías á los cristianos huidos de las misiones': 60 men under Moraga (30 Santa Bárbara, 30 San Diego), Moraga to submit a written plan: Prov. St. Pap., Benicia Mil. (C-A 17), orig. pp. 421–22 / Savage pp. 228–29, scan n227–n228, Doc 284.

Santa Bárbara muster of 1819, Comte. José de la Guerra, 1 Dec. 1819, embedding Fr. José Senán's certified burial record of the soldier Mariano Cota, killed on sentinel duty during High Mass at Pentecost 1819 by Amajahua/Mojave gentiles from the Río Colorado, and of cabo Rufino Leyva, killed the same day at San Buenaventura: Prov. St. Pap., Benicia Mil. (C-A 17), orig. pp. 227–74 / Savage p. 298, scan n297, Doc 340.

Hilario Machado to the commandants as far as Santa Bárbara, San Gabriel, 11 Oct. 1819 — warning of the Mojave approach: the Indian corporal of Sumibabi (18 leagues east) reports 20 gentiles of San Sebastián relating that an escaped captive among the Amajabas warned that the Mojaves had set out toward these missions 'a pelear y a hacer el daño posible': Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 13), tomo xx, orig. pp. 1084–85 / Savage p. 241, scan n240, Doc 306.
sources.link_note: link probable, not confirmed by the record itself

sources.citation: Solá's borrador register of outgoing orders, 1815–1822 (Monterey) — Solá orders Moraga's 1819 punitive campaign to the Mojave (Amajabat/Mongallune) ranchería, 35 cavalry and 15 Mazatlán infantry under Tte. Narciso Fabregat, 'para conocer á los gentiles la bravura de las armas del Rey'; Moraga could not reach Amajabat for lack of pasture, halting at San Joaquín and Santa Ana de Aguablanca and returning via San Gabriel, to resume next summer: Prov. St. Pap., Benicia Mil. (C-A 17), orig. pp. 152–350 / Savage pp. 118–39, scan n117–n138, Doc 177.

Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. II (San Francisco, 1885), 336–37 and 337 n.37 — 'Moraga's Unsuccessful Expedition against the Mojaves'; the march from San Gabriel on 22 November, seventy or eighty leagues into the desert, the turn-back for want of grass and water, and the return of 14 December.

Nuez, "Diario del Capellán de la Expedición para los Amajavas, 1819," MS — the chaplain Fr. Joaquín Pascual Nuez's day-by-day diary of the march, 22 Nov.–13 Dec. 1819 (Bancroft, Hist. Cal. II:337 n.37).

Gonzalez, "Experiencias," MS, 12 — the recollection of a soldier of the party, still living in 1879, that the boy killed on the return march was a servant of the padre (Bancroft, Hist. Cal. II:337 n.37).

features.notes: This feature is now fully documented from C-A — six linked manuscripts covering provocation, order of battle, campaign report and outcome. Two corrections to the feature text. (1) PLACE: the summary says 'Interior Santa Barbara.' That is wrong. Moraga marched east from Mission San Gabriel into the Mojave Desert on 22 November 1819 and turned back roughly seventy or eighty leagues out; the Santa Bárbara connection is only that the troops came from that presidio and returned to it. The map pin should be moved. (2) RETURN POINT: ca17-d299 says Fabregat and Moraga returned to Santa Bárbara on 14 December; Bancroft II:337, following Fray Nuez's diary, says Moraga reached San Gabriel on 14 December. Same date, different place — not reconciled here. Bancroft also supplies the causation the feature gestures at: the Amajavas had revenged themselves for their treatment at San Buenaventura by raiding the gentile rancherías, which is why Moraga found the interior peoples already devastated. Not linked, but noted as available: ca13-d305 (Moraga forwarding the San Gabriel and San Fernando escorts' intelligence, 12 Oct. 1819) and ca13-d368 (Moraga, 8 Jan. 1820, urging that the attempt be renewed in May when the horses are fat).

features.name: Killing of Padre Quintana at Santa Cruz
features.summary: Neophytes at Mission Santa Cruz killed Padre Andrés Quintana after he used a wire-tipped whip on them. Lorenzo Asisara's eyewitness account (recorded 1877) is the primary source. Planned conspiracy among neophytes — lured padre out at night, strangled and mutilated him. Death concealed as natural for years.
features.result: Padre killed — indigenous resistance to mission abuse

sources.citation: Lorenzo Asisara account, in Rose Marie Beebe and Robert M. Senkewicz, eds., Lands of Promise and Despair: Chronicles of Early California, 1535-1846 (Santa Clara/Berkeley: Santa Clara University/Heyday, 2001), 284-93.
Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. II (San Francisco: History Co., 1886), 387-89 and notes 43-47.
Jose Maria Amador, 'Memorias sobre la historia de California' (Bancroft dictation, taken by Thomas Savage, 1877), 77-78 — the narrative to which Lorenzo Asisara's eyewitness account is appended.

Prov. St. Pap., Benicia (Military) (BANC MSS C-A 17), scan n100-n102 / Savage 102-103, Doc 153: Tte. Jose Ma Estudillo to Gov. Arrillaga, Mission Santa Cruz, 23 Oct. 1812 — diligencias on the death of P. Fr. Andres Quintana.
Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 12), tomo xix. 1049-50, 1059-60 / scan n329, Savage 322, Doc 405: Comte. Luis Arguello to Gov. Arrillaga, San Francisco, 13 Oct. 1812 — death of Padre Quintana reported.
Prov. Rec. (BANC MSS C-A 26), tomo xi-xii. 722-23 / scan n222, Savage 222, Doc 828: Gov. Arrillaga to Bernardo Estudillo, La Soledad, 15 Oct. 1812 — order to view the body.

Prov. Rec. (BANC MSS C-A 26), tomo xi-xii. 117-19 / scan n33, Savage 34, Doc 108: [Gov. Sola] to Capt. de la Guerra, Monterey, 28 Mar. 1816 — the sentences.
Prov. Rec. (BANC MSS C-A 25), tomo ix. 470-76 / scan n390-n391, Savage 387-388, Doc 697: Sola register entries, 1816 — sentences in the Quintana causa; Sola to the Viceroy, 5 Apr. 1816.
Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 13), tomo xx. i.470-71 / scan n116, Savage 117, Doc 133: Guerra y Noriega to Gov. Sola, Santa Barbara, 17 Apr. 1816 — receipt of the five convicted Indians.

Sta Cruz, Libro de Mision, MS., 36-37 (burial certificate by P. Marquinez); Arch. Sta B., MS., xii. 93-94; Arch. Obispado, MS., 86; Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS., xxviii. 102.

features.notes: Feature carried NO ca_record; nine C-A links added. Bancroft II:387-89 footnotes name the manuscripts (Prov. St. Pap. xix.323; Prov. Rec. xi.221-2/xii.223; Prov. St. Pap., Ben. Mil. xliv.21 and xlix.59-61; Prov. Rec. ix.138-9, xi.33) and each resolves to a subject-matching C-A record above (the page-interval resolver returned only neighbourhood noise; matches made on content). Savage's own copies disagree; not harmonised. Killing date 12 Oct 1812 is independently confirmed by ca26-d108 ('noche del 12 Oct 1812').

features.name: Sánchez SF Campaign
features.summary: SF area. Solá: campaign under Sargento Sánchez "fue muy brillante." Recommended for alférez despite near-invalid status.

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap., Benicia (Military) (BANC MSS C-A 17), scan n240 / Savage 241, orig. p.455, Doc 300: Gov. Sola to Capt. de la Guerra (in Mexico), Monterey, 6 Jan. 1820 — Sanchez's expedition 'muy brillante,' recommended for alferez.

Prov. St. Pap., Benicia (Military) (BANC MSS C-A 17), scan n227-n228 / Savage 228-229, orig. pp.421-22, Doc 284: Gov. Sola to Tte. Gabriel Moraga, San Carlos, 24 Sept. 1819 — instructions forming the campaign, including the San Francisco party under Sgt. Sanchez.

Prov. St. Pap., Benicia (Military) (BANC MSS C-A 17), scan n231-n232 / Savage 232-233, orig. pp.425-30, Doc 288: Gov. Sola to Capt. de la Guerra, [Monterey], 7 Oct. 1819 — approves each presidio mounting its own expedition within its district.
sources.link_note: link probable, not confirmed by the record itself

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. II (San Francisco: History Co., 1886), 334-36 and notes 31-32.

Jose Maria Amador, 'Memorias sobre la historia de California' (Bancroft dictation, 1877), 15-16; P. Narciso Duran to Sola, 2 June and 28 Oct. 1819, Archivo del Arzobispado, MS., iii. pt. ii. 82-84, 104-5; Guerra, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS., iv. 45, 49, 51-52.

features.notes: DATE CORRECTION: the feature is dated 1820, but the campaign ran in OCTOBER 1819; ca17-d300 (6 Jan 1820) is Sola's retrospective praise and promotion recommendation, presumably the source of '1820'. Bancroft II:335 has the march 'early in October' 1819 and the force back before the end of the month. NAME/PLACE DISCREPANCY: ca17-d300 calls it Sgt. Sanchez's 'Santa Cruz-direction' expedition, while ca17-d284 (the order forming it) and Bancroft both send Sanchez's San Francisco party through San Jose into the lower San Joaquin. Savage's rubric and the operational order disagree; flagged, not reconciled. No C-A record of Sanchez's own battle report was found: Bancroft says of the northern expeditions 'we know little more than the fact that they were made.'

features.name: Battle of Punta de Guijarros (Lelia Byrd)
features.summary: FIRST NAVAL ENGAGEMENT in California. Shore battery vs. American frigate. Grapeshot exchanged; ship escaped.

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 11), tomo xviii. 633-36 / scan n256-n262, Savage 255 [stamp] / 252 [hand], Doc 290: Manuel Rodriguez, comandante of San Diego, to Gov. Arrillaga, 10 Apr. 1803 (certified copy, Loreto 12 May 1803) — 'Sobre lo acaecido con tripulantes de Fragata Lelia Bird.'

Prov. Rec. (BANC MSS C-A 25), scan n270-n271, Savage 268/20, orig. p.66, Doc 501: Governor of the Californias to the Viceroy, Loreto, 1 May 1803 — forwards the San Diego comandante's parte on the Lelia Bird.

features.notes: SERIOUS DATE PROBLEM. I read the leaf images (C-A 14 n163-n164). The battery item sits inside a letter whose Savage heading reads '179[2] - Dic.e 24 - (No dice el lugar) / Arrillaga al Com.te Gral. (10 Docs) - pp. 384-7.' The final year digit is formed identically to the '2' of 'Dic.e 24' on the same line, and the letter's other items are unambiguously 1792: the Sutil, Mexicana, Saturnina and Activo anchoring at Monterey on 22 Sept. from the exploration of the Strait of Juan de Fuca (the Galiano-Valdes voyage of 1792) and Bodega y Cuadra sailing on 14 Oct. So the battery was ordered and built in AUTUMN 1792 and reported 24 Dec. 1792 — not October 1794 (the feature) and not 1793 (the catalog date on ca14-d139). ca14-d78 carries the same 1794/1792 problem. Recommend re-dating the feature and re-checking both catalog dates against the leaf.

Padre Rodríguez stayed — "no disposition to molest him."
features.result: INDIGENOUS VICTORY — Chumash held fortified mission for 29 days

features.name: Recapture of La Purísima
features.summary: Lt. Estrada: 109 men (16 artillery, 23 cavalry, 35 infantry, 35 Indian auxiliaries) + 4-pounder. 8 AM attack. 400 neophytes returned fire from cannon, swivels, muskets + arrows. Neophyte guns ineffective — "ignorance of gunners." Canon may have burst, killing defenders. Cavalry cut off escape. P. Rodríguez interceded. Over at 10:30 AM. Indians: 16 killed, many wounded. Spanish: 3 wounded (1 mortal). 7 sentenced to death + shot. 4 ringleaders: 10 yrs exile.
features.result: Mexican victory — 2.5 hour battle; 7 Chumash leaders executed

features.name: Estanislao's First Revolt — Sánchez Defeated
features.summary: ESTANISLAO — "a neophyte of more than ordinary ability, educated at Mission San José, of which establishment he was at one time alcalde." Ran away 1827-28 with CIPRIANO. By Nov 1828 PP. Durán and Viader warned Martínez of general rising. Earlier ~20-man expedition accomplished nothing. Estanislao continued "insulting challenges to the soldiers." May 5-8: Alf. Sánchez with ~40 men + damaged swivel-gun. Divided into 6 parties of 6 under Cpls. Piña, Berreyesa, Soto. 2 of Piña's men "so rash as to enter the wood" — killed. "Ammunition exhausted, men tired out, weather excessively hot." Estanislao left unconquered. Cpl. Soto and pvts. Peña and Pacheco praised for gallantry.
features.result: INDIGENOUS VICTORY — Sánchez's force repulsed with heavy losses (~50% casualty rate)

quote.es: Duhaut-Cilly claims Sánchez "could not get at the Indian warriors, but killed 30 women and children, and with this shameful glory returned."

(3) Bancroft flagged his order-date as suspect ('May 6th, probably an error in date'); the C-A copy reads 8 May 1829, still after Sánchez's 5 May departure. features.name: Estanislao's Revolt — Vallejo's Expedition
features.summary: VALLEJO'S 3RD COMMAND — prior campaigns: Sierra Nevada from S. Miguel (1 killed, 15 wounded), Tulares (35 men, "slain 48 Indians, no casualties"). 107 men + 3-pounder. Set impenetrable wood on fire. Sánchez with 25 men fought 2+ hrs in burning wood. Vallejo with 37 men found "pits and ditches arranged with considerable skill" — "Indians could never have been dislodged except by the agency employed." Pursued to Arroyo Seco: "some negotiations" then Indians declared "they would die rather than surrender." Cut road through chaparral with axes; 8 wounded; ammunition ran out. Night: Indians escaped one by one. Morning: only dead bodies + 3 women. ATROCITY: Piña records 6+ captives killed. Osio: "order of no quarter given by Vallejo, infuriated auxiliaries wrought terrible carnage, pits for defences utilized as graves." Fiscal concluded: only 1 man + 1 woman killed — woman "unjustifiably by soldier Joaquín Alvarado." Martínez: "no decisive results obtained." Pardoned Oct 7, 1829.
features.result: Pyrrhic Mexican victory — Estanislao escaped; atrocity investigation

quote.en: YOSCOLO CONNECTION: Davis reports Yoscolo later seized 200 girls from Sta Clara, joined Estanislao in Mariposa. Vallejo "outgeneralled by the Indians." Yoscolo's head later displayed on pole at Sta Clara.
