features.notes: Two discrepancies to flag, not reconciled. (1) CASUALTIES: the map text (from Bancroft) says the fiscal found 'only 1 man + 1 woman killed'; Vallejo's own report (ca53-d9) states 'several rebels + 3 women killed, 3 women captured' and 11 men + 2 auxiliaries wounded. Savage's abstract of Vallejo and the fiscal's finding do not agree, and Bancroft prints both without resolving them. (2) DATES: the map header reads 'May 29 - Jun 4, 1829'; ca53-d9 says the force set out 26 May with 107 men, a cannon and 2,500 cartridges, and the report is dated at San José 4 June. Bancroft's 29 May is the San Joaquin crossing, not the departure. Also note ca19-d47's catalogue summary hedges the commander's forename ('Gonzalo?'); the hedge is resolved by the record's own content, which names soldier Alvarado exactly as Bancroft's footnote does.

features.name: Vallejo vs. Guapos (Sotoyomes)
features.summary: VALLEJO'S SONOMA FRONTIER. Cainameros (allies near Sta Rosa) attacked by Sotoyomes/"Guapos" — 22 killed, 50 wounded. Chiefs appealed to Vallejo. Apr 1: 50 soldiers + 100 Indians + Cainamero force. Salvador Vallejo commanded one division. Apr 4: Battle in Geyser region hills. Guapos "routed and driven back to their rancherías, where most of them were killed." Apr 7: back at Sonoma, zero casualties. Jun 7: TREATY with 7 tribes (Yoloytoy, Guilitoy, Ansactoy, Liguaytoy, Aclutoy, Churuptoy, Guapos). Approved by Gov. Chico. 1837: Chief Zampay of Yoloytoy revolted — captured by Solano + Salvador Vallejo; eventually became "peaceful citizen and industrious farmer."
features.result: Decisive Mexican victory — zero casualties; 7-tribe treaty followed

quote.en: Bancroft: Vallejo's Indian policy "excellent and effective when compared with any other policy ever followed in California."

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. IV: 1840-1845 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), 70-72.

Dep. St. Pap., Benicia (Military) (C-A 20), tomo lxxxi. 530 / Savage 237, scan n236, Doc 279. Gov. Mariano Chico (San Gabriel) to Mariano G. Vallejo, 27 June 1836 - approves the treaties Vallejo made on the northern frontier with several Indian tribes.
Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS. (BANC MSS C-B), iii. 104 - Vallejo's orders for assembling troops, 28 March 1836.
Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS. (BANC MSS C-B), iii. 105 - report of the campaign, 8 April 1836 (Salvador Vallejo commanded one division).
Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS. (BANC MSS C-B), iii. 193 - Comandante General Gutiérrez thanks Lt. Vallejo and his men for their gallantry, 21 April 1836.
Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS. (BANC MSS C-B), iii. 119, 217 - the treaty of 7 June 1836 with the chiefs of seven tribes.
No C-A manuscript located for the battle of 1-7 April 1836 in the Geyser region.

features.notes: The existing citation 'Dept. St. Pap. Ben. Mil. LXXXI.25-7' does resolve into C-A 20, but the only record in that neighbourhood whose content concerns the treaty is ca20-d279, Chico's approval of 27 June 1836. I found NO record carrying the text of the seven-tribe treaty of 7 June 1836 itself; I checked ca20-d275 through ca20-d288 individually and they are musters, pay budgets, mail arrangements and recruiting notes. The treaty text is therefore either unabstracted by Savage or survives only in Vallejo, Doc., iii. 119, 217. Second flag: I could find NO C-A record of the 1-7 April 1836 battle in the Geyser hills. Bancroft himself cites only Vallejo Documentos for it, which is consistent with the Sonoma frontier's operational correspondence living in C-B rather than C-A.

features.name: Battle of Soscol — Horse Thieves
features.summary: 50 Indian horse-thieves crossed Sacramento, appeared at Soscol with band of tame horses, aiming to stampede Sonoma horses. 34 killed in battle with Vallejo's men; rest surrendered. Chief CUMUCHÍ shot at Sonoma for his crimes.
features.result: Decisive Mexican victory — 34 killed, 0 Mexican casualties

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. IV: 1840-1845 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), 72-73.

Dept. St. Pap. (C-A 29), tomo iv. 498-501 / Savage 223, scan n220, Doc 253. Mariano G. Vallejo (Sonoma) to Juan Bautista Alvarado, 7 August 1838 - reports the August 1838 encounter with predatory Indians, prisoners taken, and asks to found a new establishment to contain the depredations.
sources.link_note: link probable, not confirmed by the record itself

sources.citation: Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS. (BANC MSS C-B), v. 124 - Vallejo's circular to the authorities, 3 August 1838, with Cumuchí's confession about the droves of stolen horses on the Sacramento in charge of the Moquelumnes.

features.notes: DISCREPANCY, flagged not reconciled: Bancroft (from Vallejo, Doc., v. 124) gives 34 killed and names the executed chief Cumuchí; the C-A record, Vallejo's own letter of 7 August 1838, says only 'tuvo un encuentro con algunos Indios depredadores y mataron algunos' and that he holds some prisoners. Savage's abstract carries no number and no chief's name. I regex-grepped the entire catalogue for Cumuchi / Cumuchí / Soscol / Suscol and got zero hits, so the name Cumuchí and the figure 34 rest solely on the C-B circular. Note also that the map dates the engagement to August 1838 and places it at Soscol; Vallejo's C-A letter is dated Sonoma, 7 August 1838 and does not name the place.

features.name: Capture of Zampay (Yoloytoy)
features.summary: Chief ZAMPAY of the Yoloytoy broke the 1836 treaty, "committing many outrages and trying to arouse the Sotoyomes again." Head chief MOTI offered to aid his capture. Combined forces of SOLANO and SALVADOR VALLEJO effected capture. Zampay held captive at Sonoma but eventually "became a peaceful citizen and industrious farmer."

quote.en: Before this expedition Vallejo organized a company of 44 Suisunes and Napas, "armed and equipped like Mexican soldiers," under Lt. Sabas Fernandez, given to Solano as bodyguard.

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. IV: 1840-1845 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), 72.
Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS. (BANC MSS C-B), iv. 250, 256 - M. G. Vallejo to his brothers Salvador and Jesús, 25-26 June 1837.
Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS. (BANC MSS C-B), xxxii. 104 - Alvarado thanks Salvador Vallejo for his gallant achievement, 26 July 1837.
Salvador Vallejo, Notas Históricas sobre California, MS., 7-65 (Bancroft Library dictation).
Mariano G. Vallejo, Recuerdos Históricos y Personales (Historia de California), MS., iii. 230-38, 298-99, 299-304 (Bancroft Library dictation).
No C-A manuscript located for the capture of Zampay, June 1837.

features.notes: This is a recorded null for the C-A series. Every manuscript Bancroft cites for the Zampay episode is in the Vallejo Documentos (C-B) or is a Bancroft dictation. The map's existing citation is already correct as to collection; my only correction is that it is not a C-A citation and should not be expected to yield an archivesofcalifornia.com link.

features.name: Sacking of Pacheco/Sánchez Ranchos
features.summary: Indians sacked ranchos of Pacheco and Sánchez near San Juan Bautista: killed 1 white man, "outraging several women, burning the buildings, and destroying all they could lay their hands on." Sánchez rancho also attacked March 1837 (2 Indians killed). Riflemen at Monterey demanded $2 each before pursuing.

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. IV: 1840-1845 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), 75-76.
Dept. St. Pap. (C-A 29), tomo iv. 468-469 / Savage 213-214, scan n210-n211, Doc 238. Antonio María Osio (Monterey) to his cousin [José Castro], 24 July 1838 - 'Relativo á depredaciones de Indios'.
Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS. (BANC MSS C-B), v. 116-17, 129.
Hartnell, Narrativa, MS., 5 (Bancroft Library dictation); Mariano G. Vallejo, Historia de California, MS., iii. 378-80.

features.notes: Partial coverage, flagged. Osio's letter (ca29-d238) attests the Pacheco rancho attack - one gente de razón killed and several wounded - and adds two murders at Hartnell's rancho that Bancroft does not mention in his text. It does NOT mention the Sánchez rancho, the sexual assaults, or the burning of the buildings; those details come from Vallejo, Doc., v. 116-17, 129 and from Hartnell's Narrativa. So this record confirms the engagement but not every element of the map's summary. Note also that Bancroft's footnote cites Hartnell, Narrativa, MS., 5 - and Osio's letter is the contemporaneous report of the killings at Hartnell's own rancho, an independent corroboration Bancroft did not use.

features.name: Death of Yozcolo at Santa Clara
features.summary: Party of YOZCOLOS attacked neophytes guarding wheat-fields at Santa Clara, killing 1. Leader DIOSCULO/YOZCOLO was killed and "his head set up on a pole at the mission." This is the same Yoscolo linked to Estanislao by Davis — confirmed ex-neophyte resistance leader.

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. IV: 1840-1845 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), 76.

Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS. (BANC MSS C-B), viii. 4, 41; and viii. 46 (21 August 1839, a 75-man party returned to San José from the pursuit of eleven runaways, two killed).
No C-A manuscript located for the death of Yozcolo at Santa Clara, July 1839. Bancroft's 'St. Pap., Miss., MS., ix. 60-1' does not resolve to a Santa Clara record in C-A 51.

features.notes: Recorded null with a positive finding about the citation. The map's existing citation 'St. Pap., Miss., MS., ix. 60-1' does NOT resolve to a Santa Clara document in the C-A series. I tested both possible readings of Bancroft's tomo pagination against C-A 51 and both fail, and I verified one of them against the leaf image rather than the catalogue. A user clicking this feature should be told the manuscript is not currently locatable in C-A, not sent to a wrong leaf.

features.name: Prado Mesa Ambush on Río de Estanislao
features.summary: Alf. PRADO MESA on expedition against thieves on "Río de Estanislao" (Stanislaus River). Surprised by the foe. 3 citizen volunteers killed, Mesa wounded, 6 of his men wounded, many weapons lost. Desiderio Briones left behind — found 7 days later by Francisco Palomares. "This disaster caused much excitement and alarm. The Indians became bolder than ever."
features.result: INDIGENOUS VICTORY — Mexican force routed with heavy losses

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. IV: 1840-1845 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), 76.

Dept. St. Pap., Monterey (C-A 43), tomo iv. 19 (Savage stamp 245), orig. pp. 72-73, scan n245, Doc 546. Manuel Jimeno (Monterey) to the Prefect of the 1st District, 15 December 1839 - on the 'suceso desgraciado' of alférez Prado's party against Indian horse-thieves; alférez Rafael Pinto marches with 15 soldiers to Mission San José.

Departmental Records (C-A 49), tomo x. 75 / Savage x·17, scan n172, Doc 451. Gov. Alvarado (Monterey) to the administrator of San José, 13 December 1839 - alférez Rafael Pinto sallies with 15 soldiers against the Tulare Indians.

Dept. St. Pap. (C-A 29), tomo iv. 725-26 / Savage 287, scan n282, Doc 360. Mariano G. Vallejo (Sonoma) to Gov. Alvarado, 26 December 1839 - 'Sobre depredaciones de indios en San José. Falta de fuerza pública.'
sources.link_note: link probable, not confirmed by the record itself

sources.citation: Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS. (BANC MSS C-B), xxv. 249; viii. 368, 373, 375, 382, 394-95.
San José Archives, MS., i. 43-46 (the Pueblo Papers of San José).

features.notes: This feature resolves unusually cleanly: two of Bancroft's footnote citations land on exactly the right record by their own page numbers, and a third lands one page off in the direction I verified independently for C-A 29. Note the map's date, 'December 1839', is right: the disaster is reported to Monterey by 13 December and the governor's relief order goes out the same day. None of the three C-A records gives the casualty figures; the three killed, Mesa wounded, six wounded and Desiderio Briones found seven days later all come from Vallejo, Doc., and from the San José Archives.

features.name: Sonoma Native Infantry Revolt
features.summary: Vallejo's own Indian infantry company — "about 25 selected Indians given Spanish names on the rosters, armed with muskets" — attempted revolt. "Many of the number were killed in a fight, and nine were subsequently shot." A trained indigenous military unit turned against its commanders.

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. IV: 1840-1845 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), 74.

Dept. St. Pap. (C-A 30), tomo v. 17-18 / Savage 6, scan n5, Doc 7. Mariano G. Vallejo (Sonoma), 12 April 1840 - 'Sobre sublevación de tropa': the frontier infantry company rose on the night of the 9th, meaning to destroy the cavalry and kill Chief Solano; alférez Lázaro Piña with many rancherías and gentiles under their chiefs attacked them, killed many and shot those taken.

Dept. St. Pap. (C-A 30), tomo v. 19-21 / Savage 6, scan n5, Doc 8. Mariano G. Vallejo (Sonoma) to the Jefe de las Californias, 13 April 1840 - forwards the document on what happened on the frontier, explaining that it kept him from going to San Francisco for the sailing of the ship carrying the foreign prisoners.
sources.link_note: link probable, not confirmed by the record itself

sources.citation: Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS. (BANC MSS C-B), viii. 192; xiv. 18; xxxiii. 56-57; and Vallejo, Historia de California, MS., iv. 166-68.

features.notes: DATE CORRECTION and a discrepancy. (1) The map dates this 'April 1840' with month confidence; Vallejo's own letter fixes the rising to the night of 9 April 1840, so the date can be tightened to 9-12 April 1840. (2) DISCREPANCY: Savage's abstract says the rebels were attacked by alférez Lázaro Piña together with many rancherías and gentiles under their own chiefs, who 'matan á muchos y fusilan á los cogidos' - killed many and shot those taken. It gives no number. Bancroft's 'nine were subsequently shot' comes from Vallejo, Doc., viii. 192 / xiv. 18 / xxxiii. 56-57, not from this record. (3) A detail the map omits and the manuscript supplies: the mutineers' stated aim was to destroy the cavalry and kill Chief Solano, and the force that put them down was itself largely indigenous.

features.name: CLEAR LAKE MASSACRE — Salvador Vallejo
features.summary: LARGEST SINGLE-DAY DEATH TOLL IN CALIFORNIA. Capt. SALVADOR VALLEJO: 70 Californians + 200 auxiliary Indians. 12 soldiers + 30 auxiliaries reached island of "Moth" by rafts. Night attack 8-11 PM. 170 INDIANS KILLED. Official report placed island "near Cape Mendocino" — actually Clear Lake. Bojorges: real objective was slave-raiding ("to obtain Indian laborers and servants"). Dr. Sandels: attack was "in the absence of all the fighting men." Negro deserter "shot in the back." Governor ordered investigation — result unknown. Tribes: Mottiyomi, Chiliyomi, Holiyomi, Tuliyomi, Supuyomi, + 4 more.

quote.en: Precursor to 1850 U.S. Army "Bloody Island" massacre at same lake by Lt. Nathaniel Lyon.

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. IV: 1840-1845 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), 162-63.
Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS. (BANC MSS C-B), xi. 342 - Salvador Vallejo, from Mendocino, to M. G. Vallejo, 13 March 1843, describing the previous evening's fight.

Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS. (BANC MSS C-B), xi. 354 - Col. M. G. Vallejo's report to the governor, 1 April 1843, naming the tribes (Mottiyomi, Chiliyomi, Holiyomi, Tuliyomi, Supuyomi, Paguenjelayomi, Sicomyomi, Hayomi, Clustinomayomi).
Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS. (BANC MSS C-B), xi. 361 - on the killing of the negro deserter.

Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS. (BANC MSS C-B), xi. 366 - the governor to Vallejo, 26 April 1843, ordering a strict investigation because 'the public mind is troubled about the killing of so many Indians'.
Juan Bojorges, Recuerdos sobre Historia de California, MS., 24-37 (Bancroft Library dictation).
G. M. Waseurtz af Sandels, A Sojourn in California by the King's Orphan (Sandels's narrative), for the eyewitness account of the party's return to Sonoma.
No C-A manuscript located for the Clear Lake massacre of 12-13 March 1843.

features.notes: Recorded null for the C-A series, and I want to be explicit about why: this is one of the best-documented atrocities on the map and none of its documentation is in the Archives of California. Every manuscript Bancroft used is in Vallejo Documentos (BANC MSS C-B), because the Sonoma frontier command's operational correspondence went into Vallejo's private files rather than the departmental archive. The map's existing citation is accurate as to the documents; it simply names a collection that will never yield an archivesofcalifornia.com link. Note also the geography flag Bancroft himself raises and the map repeats: Salvador Vallejo's official report placed the island near Cape Mendocino, and Bancroft concludes on Bojorges's evidence that the scene was Clear Lake.

features.name: Chaguanosos Steal 1,200 Horses from SLO
features.summary: CHAGUANOSOS (Shawnees from New Mexico, under Canadian chiefs, in league with trappers). Stole 1,200 horses from San Luis Obispo. "Well armed, ready for any kind of profitable adventure." Pursuers from LA saw "the foe retiring deliberately and independently" but "thought it imprudent to risk a conflict, especially when they saw that among the Chaguanosos there were more Americans than Indians."
features.result: Raiders escaped unchallenged — Mexicans too afraid to attack

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. IV: 1840-1845 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), 77.

Dept. St. Pap., Angeles (C-A 34), Prefecturas y Juzgados tomo iv, doc pp. 316-318, scan n506, Doc 1248. Circular from the Santa Bárbara administration to San Fernando and Los Angeles, 26 April 1840, relaying San Luis Obispo's report of the 24th that a party of Chaguanosos drove off several caballadas.

Dept. St. Pap., Monterey (C-A 43), tomo iv. 21 (Savage stamp 247), orig. pp. 87-88, scan n247, Doc 554. Manuel Jimeno to the Encargado del Juzgado de 1a Instancia of the 1st District, Monterey, 9 May 1840 - the Chaguanosos have stolen 1,000 horses at San Luis Obispo.

Dept. St. Pap., San José (C-A 45), orig. pp. 314-15 / Savage stamp 250, hand 71, scan n251, Doc 83. Manuel Jimeno to the juez of San José, Monterey, 9 May 1840 - heading 'Chaguanosos': the Chaguanoso rustlers entered the San Luis Obispo establishment, took more than 1,000 animals and threatened the servants.

Departmental Records (C-A 49), tomo xi. 69 / Savage xi·14, scan n219, Doc 562. Casarín to the juez of San Luis Obispo, Monterey, May 1840 - pursue the 'extranjeros chaguanosos' who stole more than 1,000 head.

Departmental Records (C-A 49), tomo xi. 63-65 / Savage xi·12, scan n217, Doc 557. Casarín to the juez de paz of San José, Monterey, 27 April 1840 - orders him to coordinate with Castro to pursue the Chaguanosos.
sources.link_note: link probable, not confirmed by the record itself

sources.citation: Dept. St. Pap., Angeles (C-A 34), Prefecturas y Juzgados tomo iv, doc pp. 426-429, scan n525-n526, Doc 1292. Tiburcio Tapia to the jueces de paz 1o and 2o, 23 May 1840 - a 10-man advance guard sent to observe the enemy; the raiders had gone with the caballada and darkness prevented tracking; the pursuit party inventoried at 13 men, 4 muskets, 7 pairs of pistols, 19 lances, 22 sabres, 445 cartridges.

Dept. St. Pap., Angeles (C-A 34), Prefecturas y Juzgados tomo iv, doc pp. 430-432, scan n526, Doc 1293. Ignacio Palomares (San Bernardino) to the juez de paz, 19 May 1840 - combat report: of a 23-man party, in an attack on the Chaguanosos there were deaths; he broke off as tired horses let his men fall to the raiders.

Dept. St. Pap., Angeles (C-A 34), Prefecturas y Juzgados tomo iv, doc pp. 461-469, scan n533-n534, Doc 1308. Juan Bautista Leandri to the Prefect, May 1840 - three documents including the campaign report of 30 May: the 36-man party under José Antonio Carrillo returned the night of the 28th; on the 25th it overtook the thieves at the paraje 'agua de Ramón' about 100 leagues out; 'El número de ladrones que componía la retaguardia era la de 20 hombres Ciudadanos de los Estados Unidos.'
sources.link_note: link probable, not confirmed by the record itself

sources.citation: Dept. St. Pap., Angeles (C-A 34), Prefecturas y Juzgados tomo iv, doc pp. 492-498, scan n539-n540, Doc 1321. Felipe Lugo to the Prefect, 9 June 1840 - transcribes Carrillo's campaign parte: the 36-man party set out at 3 a.m. on 23 May, tracked raiders who had a four-day start with about 3,000 head; the rearguard, surprised just before sunset at 'agua de Ramón', 'se componía de 20 hombres todos rifleros' and fled headlong, abandoning gear and about 500 cattle dead of hunger and thirst; not pursued further for the bad state of the horses and want of provisions.
sources.link_note: link probable, not confirmed by the record itself

sources.citation: Dept. St. Pap., Benicia, Prefecturas y Juzgados, MS., vi. 69-70; Duflot de Mofras, Exploration du Territoire de l'Oregon, i. 379.

features.notes: This is the richest feature in the batch: nine C-A records, two of them matching Bancroft's footnote page citations exactly. NUMBERS DISCREPANCY, flagged not reconciled: the map and Bancroft say 1,200 horses; the two governor's circulars of 9 May 1840 (ca43-d554, ca45-d83) say 1,000 and 'mas de 1000 bestias'; Casarín's order (ca49-d562) says 1,000+; and Carrillo's own campaign parte (ca34-d1321, ca34-d1308) says the raiders were driving about 3,000 head and lost more than half of them, abandoning about 1,500 dead animals. The manuscripts do not support a single figure. DATE: the map says April 1840; the San Luis Obispo report is dated 24 April, relayed 26 April, and the governor's circulars follow on 9 May, with the Los Angeles pursuit running 19-30 May. CORRECTION to the map's claim that the pursuers never engaged: ca34-d1293 records Palomares's party of 23 actually attacking the Chaguanosos with deaths on the field before he broke off, and ca34-d1307 records him recovering the caballadas beyond the Matanceras with one man wounded and one unaccounted for. Bancroft's 'thought it imprudent to risk a conflict' describes Carrillo's later party, not Palomares's.

features.name: Indian Attacks near San Diego
features.summary: Late-period indigenous military action near San Diego. Juana Machado's firsthand account describes continued frontier violence in the Mexican period.

sources.citation: Rose Marie Beebe and Robert M. Senkewicz, eds., Lands of Promise and Despair: Chronicles of Early California, 1535-1846 (Santa Clara and Berkeley: Santa Clara University / Heyday Books, 2001), 413-19 - the Juana Machado account.

Dept. St. Pap., Angeles (C-A 37), orig. pp. 420-424 / Savage 86-89, scan n87-n90, Doc 188. Agustín V. Zamorano to the ayuntamiento, San Diego, 29 May 1837 - the Jacum battle and the call for a general expedition.

Dept. St. Pap., Angeles (C-A 34), Prefecturas y Juzgados, doc pp. 437-38, scan n281-n282, Doc 676. José Antonio Estudillo (San Diego) to the Juez 1er Constitucional, 26 June 1837 - San Diego forms a 23-man guard to repel the continual threatened invasion by the sierra Indians, who 'han devastado, incendiado los ranchos' of the district.

Dept. St. Pap., Angeles (C-A 37), orig. pp. 433-434 / Savage 92, scan n93, Doc 193. Gov. Alvarado to the alcalde, Santa Bárbara, 3 August 1837 - aid Capt. Pablo de la Portilla with every resource 'para la persecución de los indios que han cometido depredaciones en Sn Diego'.

Dept. St. Pap., Angeles (C-A 37), tomo xii. 212-214 / Savage xii·17, scan n198, Doc 463. Manuel Jimeno to Tapia, Monterey, 22 November 1837 - 'Sublevación de gentiles en la frontera Sur (S. Diego)': approves the measures for defending the port of San Diego; the Comandante de la Frontera reported the invasion without stating its causes, which Padre Caballero and the comandante are to report.

Dept. St. Pap., Angeles (C-A 37), tomo xii. 234-236 / Savage xii·22, scan n203, Doc 473. Manuel Jimeno to the Prefect of the 2nd District, Monterey, 7 November 1837 - 'Sobre medidas contra indios sublevados en San Diego'.
sources.link_note: link probable, not confirmed by the record itself

features.notes: Two things the map should know. (1) This feature is a generic container ('Late-period indigenous military action near San Diego, 1837') resting on a single printed testimonio. The C-A series documents that year on the San Diego frontier in detail, and I have supplied five records that between them give a chronology: the Jacum battle of May 1837, the 23-man guard formed at San Diego in June, Alvarado's August order to reinforce Portilla's pursuit, and the November rising of the sierra gentiles. (2) ca37-d188 is not a background paper, it is the record of a distinct engagement in which the Californio force was beaten - 'QUEDÓ EL CAMPO PR LOS ENEMIGOS'. If the map carries or should carry a separate 'Battle of Jacum, 1837' feature, that record belongs to it, and linking it here is second best. I have flagged it rather than quietly folding it in. Note also that the Juana Machado testimonio is a Bancroft Library dictation ('Los tiempos pasados de la Alta California') that Beebe and Senkewicz translate and print; the map cites the printed book, which is correct as it stands.

features.name: Indian Attacks near Guadalupe
features.summary: Late frontier violence near Guadalupe (Santa Barbara County). José Luciano Espinosa and María Gracia accounts describe indigenous raids in the final years before American conquest.

sources.citation: Rose Marie Beebe and Robert M. Senkewicz, eds., Lands of Promise and Despair: Chronicles of Early California, 1535-1846 (Santa Clara and Berkeley: Santa Clara University / Heyday Books, 2001), 420-27 - the José Luciano Espinosa and María Gracia accounts.
No C-A manuscript located for an Indian attack near Guadalupe, Santa Barbara County, in 1840.

features.notes: A GEOGRAPHY FLAG that the map's owner needs to resolve before any link is attached. The feature is plotted at 34.97 / -120.57, which is Guadalupe in Santa Barbara County (Rancho Guadalupe, near Santa Maria), and the summary glosses it that way. I could not find a single C-A record of an Indian attack at that Guadalupe in any year, let alone 1840: I grepped the whole catalogue for Arellanes, Nipomo, Rancho Guadalupe and Olivera, and listed every 1840 record mentioning Santa Bárbara, San Luis Obispo or La Purísima, and the 1840 material for that stretch of coast is entirely the Graham affair, the Carrillo conspiracy depositions, and presidial musters. The ONLY 'Indian attack near Guadalupe' documented in the corpus is at Mission Guadalupe del Norte on the BAJA CALIFORNIA frontier, in the San Diego demarcation - about 500 miles south of where the pin sits. Two candidate records are named in my evidence below, deliberately NOT emitted as links. Someone should check Beebe and Senkewicz pp. 420-427 to see which Guadalupe José Luciano Espinosa and María Gracia are actually talking about; if it is the Baja mission, both the pin and the summary's 'Santa Barbara County' gloss are wrong. Second, smaller flag: the map dates the feature 1840 with year confidence, while the Baja Guadalupe siege records are dated 1839.

features.name: Castillo de San Joaquín fires on the Saturnina (friendly fire)
features.summary: Earliest known shore-battery firing at San Francisco. Hermenegildo Sal's guard sighted a sail at 8 a.m. and fired a warning shot; getting no reply, manned the Cantil Blanco battery (8 cannon — the future Castillo de San Joaquín / Fort Point) intending to sink her, and fired 8 cannon-shots from 11 a.m. until 5 p.m. Pilot Juan Carrasco then identified her as the Spanish navy schooner Saturnina, carrying Bodega y Quadra's Nootka dispatches, driven in for water.
features.result: Friendly-fire blunder — predates the 1803 Lelia Byrd as a battery-fires-on-ship episode

sources.citation: State Papers, Sacramento (C-A 55), tomo i. 304-5 / scan n68-69, Doc 130 - Hermenegildo Sal (San Francisco) to Gob. Arrillaga, 10 Sept. 1792, 'Haber hecho fuego contra un buque espanol por equivocacion.'

features.notes: Bancroft NULL RESULT (recorded per the null-results rule): grepped vol1 for Saturnina, Carrasco, 'by mistake', 'fired upon' and read I:490-532. Bancroft nowhere narrates this friendly-fire episode, so there is no book source and no footnote to mine. The one Saturnina passage (I:532) is Borica's 1794 gulf voyage. Vessel identity corroborated but NOT linked: ca6-d141 has the goleta Saturnina 'procedente de Nuca' as the Limites-expedition schooner, ca6-d199 gives her alias 'La Orcasitas'.

features.name: English ships at Bodega Bay (Indian intelligence)
features.summary: An Indian "de las Islas" reports two ships at Puerto de la Bodega, ashore 4 days taking water and wood, hunting deer, and trading otter skins for cattle; the sailors believed English. Sal to Arrillaga. Foreign use of unguarded Bodega as the back door to SF Bay during the Nootka-crisis / Vancouver season. Related to #41 (1793 English ship at Bodega with cannons on land).
features.result: Coastal-defense intelligence — consecutive-year foreign presence at the bay Spain meant to occupy

sources.citation: State Papers, Sacramento (C-A 55), tomo i. 296 / scan n66-67, Doc 124 - Hermenegildo Sal (San Francisco) to Gob. Arrillaga, 8 Oct. 1792, 'Buques ingleses en Bodega.'

features.name: The "Sochem" engagement
features.summary: After gentiles killed a Christian Indian of Mission San Miguel, an alférez + 5 soldiers seized 3 of the killers; on the return ~300 armed Indians attacked the patrol. The soldiers killed 1, wounded 2 and withdrew, but the alférez's horse was killed and the 3 captives escaped. Grajera then fortified against a feared assault on the mission.

sources.citation: Provincial State Papers (C-A 7), tomo xiii. 507-509 / scan n441-442, Doc 567 - Antonio Grajera (San Diego) to Gob. Borica, 13 May 1795: clash at the rancheria 'Sochem' behind Mission San Miguel.

DISCREPANCIES flagged, not reconciled: (1) the rancheria is 'Sochem' in ca7-d567 but 'Jacom' in ca24-d570; (2) attacker strength ~300 in ca7-d567 vs ~200 in ca24-d223, ca24-d570 and Bancroft; (3) Bancroft dates it 'May or June 1795' and 'June', the C-A records 17-18 Apr 1795. Bancroft's footnote page arithmetic (Prov. Rec. v. 227-8, Prov. St. Pap. xiii. 215-16) does not resolve to these records; the links rest on content, not page match.

features.name: San Luis Obispo Indian conspiracy
features.summary: A thwarted mission uprising: instigators Miguel and Marito used beads as recruitment currency; La Purísima gentiles were jailed and set to forced labor; the commandant downplayed it. Part of the 1794 unrest arc with the Santa Clara / SF crisis (#43); recurs in Arrillaga's "Estado de las Californias" (ringleaders sent to SF-fort forced labor).

features.name: The Charquín uprising at Mission San Francisco
features.summary: The Christian Indian Charquín rebelled at Mission San Francisco, took up arms against the mission Christians, and held ~20 mission women and children captive in the sierra; reported by Sgt. Miguel Pacheco. An early-1790s armed mission revolt led by a baptized Indian — a precursor to the Bay Area resistance cluster (#7 / #9).

features.name: Capture & execution of the outlaw Pomponio
features.summary: From Ignacio Martínez's hoja de servicios: with only a cabo + 2 soldiers he ran down and captured the cimarrón Christian José/Pomponio at the cañada de Novato after a firefight (one comrade wounded). Guilty of "innumerables robos, homicidios" (one victim a soldier), Pomponio was shot at Monterey by government order. The death sentence survives in C-A 17 Doc 389, a Consejo de Guerra condemning him for killing soldado Manuel Varela.
features.result: Spanish counter-banditry — Pomponio executed at Monterey

I judge the catalog's 1821 year very likely a mis-dating, but I have not seen the leaf, so I am not overwriting it. features.name: The Solís Revolt
features.summary: A convict-sergeant pronunciamiento: presidiario Sgt. Joaquín Solís and subcomisario José Mª Herrera seized Monterey against Gov. Echeandía; marched south; the SF garrison fired a salute and raised the flag to welcome them; defeated at Santa Bárbara (Pacheco's counter-revolution). Leaders deported to San Blas on the Volunteer. Prosecution built a "revolución por España" charge and named a foreign-merchant circle (Hartnell/Spence/Anderson/Stearns) on both sides.
features.result: Mexican-period military coup — suppressed; leaders deported

features.name: Post-Victoria Civil War (Ávila/Sánchez vs. Zamorano)
features.summary: After Gov. Victoria's overthrow, Vicente Sánchez and the convict José Antonio Ávila armed a band of presidiarios (weapons from Santa Bárbara) against Zamorano's northern faction. Ávila's party split from Sánchez past San Buenaventura and surrendered at Mission Santa Inés; dismissed under the 25 Apr 1832 amnesty. The endpoint of the Solís→anti-Victoria arc.

Sac. x.100) do not reconcile with Savage's running pagination; matches below rest on content and date.

features.notes: ⚠ HONEST LIMIT: this engagement rests on ONE document, a retrospective service record compiled two years later. I searched for corroboration and did not find it: content searches on San Fernando + sublevacion/cabecillas/pacificacion for 1828 across all volumes, a sweep of C-A 47 (Departmental Records, the 1828 outgoing register) for San Fernando, and a read of Bancroft III's San Fernando material returned no independent account of a July 1828 rising or of prisoners brought to Santa Barbara. The two C-A 47 items below are offered as PROBABLE context only — same mission, same fortnight, same correspondents — not as attestation of the military action.

features.name: San Diego Indian-uprising conspiracy
features.summary: A planned assault on the SD presidio — "acabar con los blancos p[ar]a ser independientes, y gobernarse ellos mismos" — extending to the missions up to San Gabriel. Ringleaders Molina and Tesochi got 2 years (attenuated for "ignorancia"); the authorities conceded "la probabilidad de los malos tratamientos" as motive. Figueroa confirmed 22 Nov 1833.

features.name: New Mexico horse-thief expedition into the Tulares
features.summary: After New Mexico "aventureros/ladrones" (allied with Tulares gentiles) drove off ~1,000 head (incl. 108 mules from Mission San Miguel; SLO stock recovered near Arroyo Grande), Gov. Figueroa ordered a 15-cavalry punitive expedition under Alf. Dámaso Rodríguez "á perseguir y destruir" the band. An early Old-Spanish-Trail horse-raiding record.

sources.citation: Dep. St. Pap., Benicia (Military) (C-A 19), tomos lxix-lxxvii, Doc 232 (orig. p.334 / Savage p.435, scan n440): Gen. Figueroa's formal instructions to Alf. Damaso Antonio Rodriguez for the punitive expedition into the Tulares, 1833.

features.notes: Bancroft narrates this affair at Hist.Cal. iii. 395-97, naming 'a grand military expedition sent out under Alferez Damaso Rodriguez.' His footnote cites 'Nuevo Mexico, Expediente de Abigeato, 1833, MS.', Los Angeles Arch. iv. 73, 86-7 and Dept. St. Pap., Angeles i.109, xi.3-4 - none of which resolved to a C-A record via q.py banc (DSP_ANG returned only ca37-d2, 1825, unrelated). The C-A 19 run is the manuscript basis regardless. Date note: Savage puts the San Miguel complaint 24 Feb 1833 and Figueroa's orders 26 Feb; d232 (the instructions) carries only a year, so the map's 'February 1833' is safe for the orders but the march itself is undated.

features.name: Felipe Briones killed at Cerro de Bolbones
features.summary: Felipe Briones killed trying to recover horses from Indians near the Cerro de Bolbones (Mt Diablo area).

sources.citation: Dept. St. Pap., Monterey (C-A 43), tomos i-viii, Doc 728, orig. pp.456-57 / scan n337: Ignacio Peralta, Rancho San Antonio, 12 Jan 1840, to the Prefecto - 'Robo de Caballada por los indios a Felipe Briones, quien los siguio con 4 hombres a los indios que lo mataron.'
Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. iv (1840-1845) (San Francisco: History Co., 1886), 76 n70.
Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS., ix. 20 (BANC MSS C-B, Bancroft Library).

features.notes: DATE DISCREPANCY, not reconciled: Bancroft (from Vallejo, Doc., MS., ix. 20) dates the killing 6 Jan 1840; the C-A record is Ignacio Peralta's report of 12 Jan 1840 from Rancho San Antonio. These are compatible (report six days after the event) but the C-A document itself carries no day for the fight, so the map should keep 'January 1840' rather than adopt 6 Jan on this record's authority. Searched q.py for 'Briones' across all volumes: the only other Briones hits are 18th-century soldiers (Marcos, Vicente, cabo Briones) and Desiderio Briones, wounded on the Estanislao in Dec 1839 - a different man and a different fight.

features.name: Martínez defeats Indians near Mt Diablo
features.summary: Lt. Martínez defeated Indians near Mt Diablo, "Marsh with other Americans rendering valuable service." Report dated Feb 7.

The 1840 C-A material on this campaign is all later in the year (ca43-d457, ca30-d22, the July patrol between San Jose and San Juan).

features.summary: Indians surrendered at a lake 30 mi south of the fort; "14 were put to death." Vallejo says a force of Californians sent to the valley multiple times rescued captives and took ~80 prisoners.

features.name: Cochrane squadron raid on Mission Todos Santos
features.summary: Ships of "la Escuadra del Lord Cochrane" entered Cabo de Cortés and attacked Mission Todos Santos at night; the inhabitants defended themselves, killing the lieutenant + 4 men, mortally wounding 3, and capturing the rest — a 13-man landing party. Gov. Solá ordered church silver withdrawn from the coast.

sources.citation: St. Pap., Sacramento (C-A 54), tomo i, Doc 149 (Savage pp.212-13 / scan n211-n212): Gov. Pablo Vicente de Sola, Monterey, 30 Mar [1823 per Savage], circular to the friars and commandants of Monterey and San Francisco - ships of 'la Escuadra del Lord Cochrane' entered Cabo San Lucas (Cabo de Cortes) and attacked Mission Todos Santos on 18 Feb; the inhabitants killed the lieutenant and four men, mortally wounded three, and captured the rest of a thirteen-man raiding party. Sola orders church silver and valuables withdrawn from the coast.

Capt. Jose Dario Arguello of Baja California via the mission cordillera; the attack on Mission San Jose del Cabo, 1 Feb, with about twelve prisoners taken by the defenders.

features.notes: The Savage copy dates Solá's circular 30 Mar 1823 and the raid itself 18 Feb; the Cochrane operations off the Californias belong to 1822, and three independent volumes (C-A 27, 55, 56) place the squadron at Cabo San Lucas in February 1822. Event year shown as circa 1822. ⚠ An earlier version of this record cited 'C-A 54 Doc 2051', a document number that no longer exists after the volume was re-itemised; the correct record is C-A 54 Doc 149. DATE DISCREPANCY, flagged not reconciled. Savage heads the C-A 54 circular '1823 Mar 30' with the raid on '18 Feb', while three other C-A records put the same raid in Feb 1822: ca27-d2 (29 Mar 1822), ca55-d84 (5 May 1822), ca56-d397 (4 May 1822). 1822 also fits Bancroft ii. 474 (the San Francisco Javier 'captured by one of Cochrane's fleet at Cape San Lucas'). Likeliest a slip of a year in Savage's heading, but I did not check the heading against the leaf, so both readings stand. Note too that the records disagree on the mission: d2 has San Jose del Cabo on 1 Feb with ~12 prisoners, d84 has both San Jose and Todos Santos sacked, d149 has Todos Santos on 18 Feb with 13 raiders - probably successive landings by one squadron.

features.name: Ambush near San Vicente / Santa Catalina
features.summary: An escort transporting 5 captured Indians was ambushed: 2 soldiers killed — Juan Camacho + one other — beaten on the head with stones, their muskets found loaded but broken; the prisoners escaped; the bodies buried at San Vicente. Distinct from #37 (the 1804 Santa Catalina Spanish victory).

Arrillaga - Muerte violenta de dos soldados pr los indios qe llevaban presos y maniatados.' Narrative: at noon on the 25th of the previous month Ruiz got the oficio from the cabo of Santa Catalina; on the 26th at 9 a.m. word came both men were dead in the Sierra de Agua Blanca. The map's note that this is distinct from #37 still holds, but they are now the same year and directly linked (see ca11-d481). The second soldier is now named: Jose Peiquera (Savage's reading; possibly Pesquera).

features.name: Spanish Yuma Punitive Campaign
features.summary: Neve and Capt. José Antonio Romeu (108 men) march down the Colorado; Romeu with 40 men and 12 Indian allies (Jalchedunes/Cocomaricopas) routs the Yuma cavalry ('crecida mortandad'), 4 soldiers wounded; Fages escorts the rescued captives. An abortive plan to re-fortify the crossing follows. Neve's 'Antecedentes de una mortandad' names the revolt's causes: gifts withheld from Palma, women seized, mules destroying the mesquite.
features.result: Spanish reprisal after the 1781 Yuma victory

Romeu (108 men) march down the Colorado.' ca22-d2019 actually reads that Neve went down with 60 men and found Romeu already holding the ruined pueblo of La Concepción WITH 108 men; the 50 soldiers + 12 settlers are a further breakdown. The '108 men' therefore belongs to Romeu's standing force, not to a joint column. Everything else in the map summary (Romeu with 40 men + 12 Indian allies, 'crecida mortandad', 4 soldiers wounded, Fages escorting the rescued captives, the abortive re-fortification of the crossing, and Neve's 'Antecedentes de una mortandad' on the revolt's causes) is confirmed verbatim across d2019, d2020 and d2024.

features.name: Tule balsa shipwreck at the Farallones
features.summary: Mission San Francisco Indians navigated by sea in tule balsas to evangelize gentiles on the opposite shore; currents carried one balsa onto the Farallones, where 2 of the 4 Indians drowned. Not a military engagement — an indigenous open-water navigation datum at the Bay mouth.

sources.citation: Pérez Fernández to Gov. Borica, 30 Nov 1794. Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 7), tomo xii–xiii, 72–73 / Savage 29–30, scan n28–n29, Doc 54.

features.notes: The catalog record places the drowning on 'the 4th of the month' in a letter of 30 Nov 1794, i.e. 4 Nov 1794 — the map's bare '1794' can be tightened to Nov 1794, but I have not read the leaf image to confirm the day, so I state it as what the catalog summary says. The record also shows the balsa voyages were not free-standing: they sit inside Pérez Fernández's refusal of extra escort soldiers for a missionary 'conquista de gentiles' across the bay toward Marin, which is the administrative context the map's 'evangelize gentiles on the opposite shore' comes from.

features.name: Horse-theft raid & punitive expedition (140-head caballada)
features.summary: 'Indios malhechores' drove off a caballada of 140 head from the national rancho; Gov. Argüello sent Alf. Santiago Argüello with 34 troops to punish the raiders and the rancherías that harbor them ('por cortar de raiz los daños'). In a related San Diego–frontier action, 14 of 15 neophyte auxiliaries who fought were killed, and ~40 raiders later burned a San Diego rancho.

features.notes: Rancherías not located in the abstract — pin placed in the Monterey-district interior, conjectural. I have not checked the leaf image, so I report what the catalog transcription says. (2) DATE/EPISODE SEPARATION: the '14 of 15 neophyte auxiliaries killed' and the ~40 raiders who burned a San Diego rancho are reported in a letter of 17 Dec 1824 to the Governor of Baja California (ca46-d212 head, ca46-d213 tail), five months after the July caballada raid and on the Baja/San Diego frontier. They may well be a distinct action, and the map's framing of them as 'related' is as far as the evidence goes. The map's date range 'Jun–Jul 1824' is confirmed: Argüello's order is 30 Jun, the raid the night of the 1st (July), the report 31 Jul 1824.

features.name: Surrender of the Spanish squadron at Monterey
features.summary: The Spanish ship-of-the-line Asia and brig Constante — Spain's last Pacific force after the loss of Peru — put into Monterey and capitulated to the Mexican Nation, their crews swearing 'el solemne juramento de sujetarse á las leyes de los Estados Unidos Mejicanos.' Argüello tapped the Asia's powder to arm the near-empty San Francisco and Monterey batteries; pilot Juan Malarín carried the acta de Capitulación to Mexico City.

features.name: The anti-Victoria revolt — the Cahuenga encounter
features.summary: California's first successful gubernatorial overthrow. The Plan of San Diego (29 Nov 1831) pronounced against Gov. Manuel Victoria 'por recobrar la representación popular'; Victoria was wounded at the Cahuenga encounter ('estado moribundo') and deported on the Pocahontas. The interregnum then splintered — the Diputación installed Pío Pico, Los Angeles proclaimed Echeandía, Zamorano rose in the north — 'casi inevitable el derramamiento de sangre.'

What the manuscripts say is different: ca57-d86 alleges Victoria was to be deported in 'la Goleta Sta Barbara, demasiado pequeña y espuesta quiza con la mira de que naufragase', while 'para alucionar al Pueblo se dijo al principio que fletaban la fragata Leonor.' features.name: The anti-Micheltorena revolt — Cahuenga/Providencia
features.summary: The last Californio overthrow of a Mexican-appointed governor. The Asamblea Departamental 'desconoce la autoridad… de M. Micheltorena,' charging his 'relaciones secretas con el extranjero Sutter' (Sutter marched for Micheltorena; M.G. Vallejo corresponded against him). Micheltorena and his cholo battalion were defeated and expelled after the Battle of Cahuenga/Providencia, installing the native-born Pío Pico as California's last Mexican governor.

features.name: Ambush of the San Diego pursuit party (Dominican frontier)
features.summary: A San Diego troop detachment pursuing Dominican-mission cimarrones (runaway neophytes) was ambushed on the Baja frontier; the action left 15 Indians dead, including a leader from Mission San Miguel — a frontier engagement in the same season as the Chumash Revolt further north.
features.result: Indigenous tactical victory over a presidial party

sources.citation: Fran.co Mª Ruiz (San Diego) to Gov. Luis Antonio Argüello, 21 Jun 1824. Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 27), Departmental State Papers, tomo I–II, orig. pp.129–131 / Savage p.37 / scan n36, Doc 43.

Gov. Luis Antonio Argüello (Monterey) to Santiago Argüello, 30 Jun 1824 — acknowledgment of the Baja-frontier action and orders to Capt. Pablo de la Portilla. Dep. Rec. (C-A 46), Departmental Records, tomo I, orig. pp.181–182 / Savage p.243 (heading), tail p.244 / scan n246–n247, Doc 335.

features.notes: Ambush site not located in the abstract — pin placed on the Dominican-mission frontier, conjectural. Bancroft does not narrate this action: grepped vols 2 and 3 for 'Fidelis', 'San Isidoro', 'fifteen Indians' — zero hits. The Baja/Dominican frontier falls outside his Alta California annals, so no book source is offered here. The two C-A records agree on all details (15 killed, the San Miguel cabecilla, the rancho house burned); ca46-d335 supplies the leader's name (Fidelis), the rancho name (San Isidoro) and the two wounded invalidos (Ignacio and Jose Lopez) that the San Diego report leaves blank.

features.name: Gentile attack on mission neophytes — '21 neophytes killed'
features.summary: A report of 21 neophytes killed by gentiles on the interior frontier of the San Diego district — evidence for the raiding-economy pressure on mission populations in the 1820s, and for inter-indigenous violence between mission and independent communities.

sources.citation: José Ignacio Bernal(?) (San José) to the Comandante, 3 Nov 1826 — reports 21 Christian Indians killed by gentiles. Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 27), Departmental State Papers, tomo I–II, orig. pp.498–500 / Savage p.~136 / scan n130, Doc 145.
Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. III (1825–1840), San Francisco: The History Company, 1886, pp.109–110 and p.110 n.51.

features.notes: Location not given in the abstract — conjectural pin in the SD interior. TWO CORRECTIONS TO THE FEATURE TEXT. (1) The feature places this 'on the interior frontier of the San Diego district'. The manuscript is written from SAN JOSÉ; the victims were Mission San José neophytes killed by gentiles in the Cosumnes/San Joaquin country. It is a northern, not a southern, episode, and it is the outrage that provoked alférez José Sánchez's Nov 1826 Cosumnes campaign (Bancroft III:110). (2) Casualty figure: the manuscript says 21; Bancroft's narrative text says 'twenty or thirty of whom were killed, or at least never returned' while his own footnote quotes the 21 from this document. Page-system note: Bancroft cites 'Dept. St. Pap., MS., i. 135', which matches the record's SAVAGE page (~136), not its original tomo page (p.498–500).

features.name: Martínez's 'campaña en los Ríos'
features.summary: Ignacio Martínez's 1827 campaign into the Delta rivers against the runaway and rebel Indians of Missions San José and Santa Clara — 2 soldiers killed. The precursor operation to the 1829 Estanislao campaigns, in the same theater.

sources.citation: Ignacio Martínez (San Francisco) to Gov. José María Echeandía, 31 May 1827 — reports the campaign 'en los Ríos'. St. Pap., Missions & Colonization (C-A 53), tomo II, orig. pp.21–23 / Savage p.12 / scan n11, Doc 8.

features.notes: NULL RESULT, recorded deliberately. I could find no second manuscript for this campaign. (a) Bancroft: grepped vol3 for 'en los Rios', 'los Rios', 'Martinez' (60+ hits read in context) and for every 'St. Pap., Miss. and Colon., MS., ii.' citation — he cites that tomo at pp.6, 91, 96, 200–308 etc. but never pp.21–23, and his 'Los Rios' references are all 1829 Estanislao, not 1827. Bancroft appears simply not to narrate this campaign. (b) DB: searched C-A 47 (Dept. Records 1827) and C-A 18 (DSP Benicia Mil., 1827) for an Echeandía reply or a service-record entry; nothing on subject. So ca53-d8 is, on present evidence, the sole record of the engagement — which is itself worth stating on the map.

features.name: Vallejo's & Sánchez's punitive horse-raid expeditions
features.summary: Stock-raid reprisal operations by Vallejo and Sánchez in the Monterey district interior, mounted while the Monterey troops were destitute (the pay-mutiny backdrop, six months before the Solís revolt).

Likewise ca48-d423 (3 Jun 1829, to the comandante of SAN FRANCISCO, on Sánchez's casualties) belongs to the failed first anti-Estanislao expedition, not to these April raids. Figure discrepancy left unreconciled: manuscript = 22 soldiers + 3 vecinos, 40 taken; Bancroft III:112 = 35 men, 48 slain, no casualties; Vallejo Doc. xx.280 (per Bancroft) = 1 killed, 15 wounded.

features.name: The great 1840 horse-raid campaign ('agua de Ramón')
features.summary: A multi-week mounted campaign, not a single skirmish. Chaguanosos drove off three mare-herds from Mission San Gabriel (14 May); the LA vecino-militia mobilized (13→36 men, 4 muskets, 19 lances); Ignacio Palomares's ~23-man party was routed; relief columns held the Puerta del Cajón and recovered the herds at the 'agua de Ramón' surprise. Leandri's report: the rearguard was '20 hombres Ciudadanos de los Estados Unidos; pero tenían á más otra gente,' driving 1,000+ head, ~1,500 driven to death in flight.
features.result: Raiders routed one militia party; herds recovered at agua de Ramón

sources.citation: Juan Crispín Pérez (San Gabriel) to the Alcalde de 1ª Instancia, 14 May 1840 — the Chaguanosos drive off 3 herds of mares from the mission. Dep. St. Pap., Angeles (C-A 34), tomo Pref. y Juzg. I–IV, doc pp.408–409 / scan n522, Doc 1285.

Unsigned (San Gabriel), 17 May 1840 — the mission's contribution to the auxiliary levy. Dep. St. Pap., Angeles (C-A 34), doc p.413 / scan n523, Doc 1288.

Tiburcio Tapia, 18 May 1840 (2 docs) — Palomares's party routed; a relief force ordered out. Dep. St. Pap., Angeles (C-A 34), doc pp.416–419 / scan n524, Doc 1290.

José Antonio Carrillo & Juan Gallardo (Cañada de la Brea) to the Prefecto del 2º Distrito, 22 May 1840, headed 'Ladrones americanos'. Dep. St. Pap., Angeles (C-A 34), doc pp.449–452 / scan n530–n531, Doc 1305.
Juan Bautista Leandri to the Prefecto, 20 May 1840 — joins Palomares, reunites 26 men, moves to hold the Puerta del Cajón. Dep. St. Pap., Angeles (C-A 34), doc pp.453–456 / scan n531–n532, Doc 1306.

Juan Bautista Leandri to the Prefecto interino del 2º Distrito, 19 May 1840 — express from Rancho San José relaying Palomares's counter-attack. Dep. St. Pap., Angeles (C-A 34), doc pp.458–460 / scan n532, Doc 1307.

Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. IV (1840–1845), San Francisco: The History Company, 1886, pp.76–77 and nn.72–74; cross-referenced at vol. III, p.682.

features.notes: Pin at Cajon Pass, the campaign's hinge; 'agua de Ramón' itself is unlocated (secondary lit puts the fight at Resting Springs — the partes' 'Ramón' is a datum to weigh vs Bancroft IV:77, not to harmonize). DISCREPANCIES, flagged not reconciled. (1) Dead stock: Leandri's parte (d1308) says 'como 1500 bestias muertas'; Carrillo's parte as transcribed by Lugo (d1321) says 'como 500 reses muertas de hambre y sed'. The feature's '~1,500 driven to death' follows Leandri only. (2) Force size: d1292 gives 13 men, d1305 gives '15 good men' with 225 horses, from the same equipment list. (3) Bancroft IV:76–77 is thin and partly contradicts the manuscripts: he pins the great 1840 theft to SAN LUIS OBISPO in April (1,200 horses) and says the pursuers 'thought it imprudent to risk a conflict' — the C-A 34 E29 dossier documents the San Gabriel theft of 14 May and a real engagement at the agua de Ramón. His fn.74 ('Dept. St. Pap., Ang., MS., iv. 88–92, 97–100') resolves into this same C-A 34 neighbourhood (docs 1304–1309).

features.name: Plaza firefight (Alvarado civil war)
features.summary: Californio-vs-Californio action of the 1838 civil war (the Alvarado–Carrillo contest for the governorship): per José Castro's abstracted report, a 160-man force garrisoning 'la plaza' abandoned it by night after a 2-day continuous firefight with only 1 dead, pursued by cavalry; two bronze cannon at the Castillo were transferred to José Estrada.

(C-A 29), Departmental State Papers, tomo IV, orig. pp.419–425 / Savage pp.188–189 / scan n185–n186, Doc 228. Savage's verbatim copy.

sources.citation: 1838 Alvarado–Carrillo civil-war campaign dossier (Castro congratulated on the toma de San Buenaventura; powder and 4,000 cartridges; Alvarado to Carlos A. Carrillo naming Pablo de la Portilla and Castañeda). Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 29), tomo IV, orig. pp.435–449 / Savage pp.198–204 / scan n195–n201, Doc 230.
Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. III (1825–1840), San Francisco: The History Company, 1886, pp.552–554 ('Battle of San Buenaventura') and nn.87–90.

features.notes: 'La plaza' is not named on the leaf — probably Santa Bárbara or a southern plaza. Conjectural pin; transcribe the parte before locating or quoting. IDENTIFICATION: 'la plaza' is SAN BUENAVENTURA. Bancroft III:552–553 quotes Castro's report almost word for word — 'after two days of continuous firing, and with the loss of only one man killed on our side, the whole force of 110 men which defended this place has fled on foot under cover of night', pursuit by mounted infantry under Capt. Villa and lancers under Capt. Cota. So the feature can be titled the Battle of San Buenaventura, 27–28 Mar 1838. TWO DISCREPANCIES, not reconciled. (1) Garrison size: the C-A 43 abstract says 160 men; the C-A 29 verbatim copy and Bancroft both say ~110. (2) DATE: ca29-d228 is catalogued 1838-05-28, but Bancroft dates Castro's report 28 March 1838 and the battle 27–28 March. One of the two is a month out; this needs a leaf re-read of C-A 29 n185 before the map states a date.

features.name: Ibarra's punitive battle at Santa Isabel ('veinte pares de orejas')
features.summary: A punitive action against ~100 or more hostile Indians, routed 4 leguas to San Felipe with Kumeyaay/Cahuilla auxiliaries; 28 killed, '20 pares de orejas' cut from the dead as proof, plus a prisoner summarily executed.

sources.citation: Juan Ma. Ibarra to the Comandante General, Santa Isabel, 5 Apr. 1826. Dep. St. Pap., Benicia, Pref. y Juzg. (BANC MSS C-A 42), tomo iii, orig. pp. 683-684 / Savage 81-83, scan n312-n314, Doc 914 (Expanded Entry 26).
Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. III: 1825-1840 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), 109 and n.68.
San Diego, Libro de Mision, MS., 96 (mission register, Mission San Diego de Alcala), cited in Bancroft, History of California, III:109 n.68.

features.notes: Abstract — transcribe the parte before quoting the orejas line. Bancroft III:109 states Ibarra had TWO fights at/near Santa Isabel in April 1826, sending 18 pairs of ears in one and 20 in the other, and that three Mazatlan-squadron soldiers had been murdered just before (probable provocation). Only the 20-pair report (ca42-d914) is in the C-A database; I searched 'orejas', 'pares de orejas', 'Santa Isabel Ibarra' across all 63 volumes and found no second report — recorded as a null. Bancroft's footnote also cites 'Dept. St. Pap., MS., i. 136-7' and 'S. Diego, Lib. Mision, MS., 96'. The DSP i.136-7 interval resolves only to ca27-d43/d44 (1824-25 Chumash-revolt and Romero-expedition items) — subject mismatch, so no link emitted. The San Diego libro de mision is a mission register, not C-A.

features.notes: The existing single link under-served the citation: it named three documents and delivered one, and the one it delivered was the May intelligence report rather than Castro's 14 March report of the standoff itself. Six further C-A records on this episode were found by content search and are added. Discrepancy to flag: ca45-d62's abstract dates Castro's San Juan Bautista bando on the Fremont invasion to 13 MAY 1846, but the identically-described proclamation survives twice elsewhere (ca31-d78, ca36-d111) dated 13 MARCH 1846, and Bancroft V:19 reproduces 'Castro's proclamation of March 13th'. features.name: The Rancho San Francisco killing of 18 'indios ladrones'
features.summary: Twenty-one armed Indians were disarmed 'mañosamente,' revolted with stones and knives, and were shot — 18 dead, 2 wounded, 1 escaped: the anti-raiding apparatus at its most lethal, weeks before the conquest.

features.notes: District-court abstract — verify vs leaf before quoting. A SECOND, INDEPENDENT and fuller record of the same event was found and is added: ca39-d152, a verbatim causa/parte militar of the same date. Discrepancy between the two, not reconciled: ca42-d1219 (Sepulveda's summary to Pico) says 21 Indians, 18 dead, 2 wounded, 1 escaped unharmed; ca39-d152 (the military proceeding) says 18 indios killed, 1 taken prisoner, and reads the '2 heridos' as wounds on SALAZAR's side, with a 12-man force and 20 bows and 20 quivers confiscated. The map's date is given as '1846' with year confidence; both records date the report 26 March 1846, so the date can be tightened. Bancroft's footnote treats the affair in one sentence: '18 Ind. were killed at S. Francisco rancho, having revolted after being captured.'

features.result: Revolt suppressed judicially; the blamed officer imprisoned

Reported to the Viceroy as proof the Sonora communication could not be secured without real garrisons; the Viceroy later reviewed a printed account of the engagement.
features.result: Spanish column fought through — 7 Indians killed

features.summary: Gentiles 'de la otra banda' killed 5 Indians and 2 women of the mission rancherías; Borica sent Sgt. Macario Castro with 10 cuera soldiers, 8 Christian Indians, and 24 aggrieved gentiles; the column caught the malefactors, killed the enemy captain 'Talholostl'[?], recovered 2 women, and captured 2 — a mixed Spanish–Native punitive force whose gentile allies were the majority.
features.result: Punitive column killed the enemy captain

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. I: 1542-1800 (San Francisco: A. L. Bancroft & Co., 1884), 558-559.

features.notes: The indigenous name is uncertain on the leaf — verbatim transcription needed. CATALOGUE GAP (span defect), reported honestly: leaves n431-n433 return 0 records from q.py leaf. They sit inside the over-declared span of ca24-d842 (scan n430-440, Savage 429-439), but d842 is Borica to Viceroy Azanza, 30 Oct 1798, 'Sobre medios para impedir el deterioro de la Indiada neofita' - a different letter; ca24-d843 resumes at n434 (Savage 433 = tomo p.109). The Pelea con Indios entry therefore has NO record and cannot be linked to a doc_id. Recommend cutting an item record at n431-n432. FACTUAL DISCREPANCIES against the map text, from my own reading of the leaves: (1) the manuscript reads 'los gentiles de la Sierra habian muerto a 6 Indios y 2 mugeres de las rancherias immediatas a la mision' - SIX Indians and two women, not five; Bancroft's 'eight rancheria Indians' is 6+2. (2) The chief's name is written 'Tatilloste' in Savage's hand (Bancroft prints 'Tatillosti'); the map's 'Talholostl' is not supported by the leaf. (3) The band is named on n432 as 'esta rancheria de malhechores llamados Osos'. (4) The two recovered women are said to be of the tribe 'Ausaimes'. (5) One soldier was wounded by an arrow whose flint lodged in him. (6) The two captured gentiles were to be kept at the mission 'pa. ensenarles el espanol y pa. emplearlos de guias y interpretes'. (7) The entry closes 'p.p. 443-4', i.e. original Prov. Rec. tomo VI pp. 443-444.

features.name: The Jacum battle — capitanejo Charagui defeats the San Diego column
features.summary: Twenty-five soldados and 50 gentiles auxiliares struck Jacum; 'el capitanejo Charagui… cargó con toda su gente y rodeando nuestras tropas nos las hicieron retirar, hiriéndonos á 9 soldados y 17 indios de los auxiliares… quedó el campo pr los enemigos.' The raiders had already run off the Misión San Diego caballada. Embedded in Zamorano's extermination-rhetoric letter; aftermath, Alvarado ordered all aid to Capt. Portilla for the pursuit (Aug 1837).
features.result: Indigenous victory — the field held by Charagui's force

features.name: The "Pesquisa del neófito Domingo" Firefight
features.summary: Sgt. Pablo Antonio Cota and 12 men rode into the sierra behind Mission Santa Bárbara to extract the fugitive neophyte Domingo (a runaway of over a year who, per his ministers, "hace robos y muertes en dicha Gentilidad"). Though interpreters were sent ahead to keep them calm, the gentiles loosed arrows and wounded 3 of the party; the soldiers returned fire, leaving 3 gentiles dead and more than 8 wounded. Domingo escaped; a gentile who had accompanied him was taken prisoner. An early ex-neophyte-turned-raider case, decades before secularization.
features.result: 3 gentiles killed, 8+ wounded, 3 soldiers wounded; Domingo escaped

features.name: Gentile Attack on Mission San Rafael & the Piña Expedition
features.summary: Mission San Rafael — its founding padre Amorós dead 14 July 1832, its population collapsing (~970 to ~300) and baptisms crashing (155 to 15) — was attacked by gentiles; a punitive expedition was sent out under Lázaro Piña. Most likely the "spring 1832 San Rafael revolt" the Russians at Fort Ross heard of from fugitive-Indian informants.

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. III: 1825-1840 (San Francisco: A. L. Bancroft & Co., 1885), 716 n.18 (San Rafael, Summary of events, 1832).
Vallejo, 'Documentos para la Historia de California', MS., i. 307 - Bancroft Library, BANC MSS C-B 1 et seq. (the Vallejo Documentos collection), NOT the Archives of California.
No Archives of California record found for the 1832 gentile attack on Mission San Rafael or the Pina expedition.

features.notes: 1832 date and Piña command per Bancroft; the underlying Vallejo Documentos i.307 leaf is not yet read — treat the year as attested but not leaf-verified. Bancroft's entire authority for this feature is one line and one manuscript citation, and that manuscript is NOT in the Archives of California. I could find no C-A record of the attack or of the Pina expedition. Searches run: 'San Rafael gentiles ataque expedicion' (year 1832), 'San Rafael mision indios' (1832), 'Lazaro Pina' (all volumes). The only Lazaro Pina hit is ca20-d513 (Cabo Lazaro Pina, artillery detachment pay return, 2 Nov 1831, C-A 20) - it establishes that Lazaro Pina was the artillery corporal on the San Francisco side at the right date, but it says nothing about San Rafael and I am NOT linking it. DISCREPANCY to flag: the map summary's identification with 'the spring 1832 San Rafael revolt the Russians at Fort Ross heard of' is not in Bancroft, who gives no month; and Bancroft's own p.716 statistics note calls the 970-to-300 population collapse 'extremely unreliable... more likely there is an error in the figures', so the demographic framing in the map summary should not be presented as fact. Separately, the Pina of Bancroft III:111-113 (the 1829 Estanislao campaign) is Joaquin Pina, not Lazaro - do not conflate them.

features.name: The Bodega Mobilization under Toribio
features.summary: About 200 armed Indians — gentiles plus Christian fugitives from Mission San Rafael — massed at Bodega under Toribio (Pixpix-uccux), "armed and ready to die" rather than be seized, hosted by the Bodega chief Gualinela. Kostromitinov, the RAC manager at Fort Ross, asked Vallejo to help round up the retreating Ross Indians; Vallejo declined and pacified through Gualinela. It worked — Toribio came in peacefully seven months later.
features.result: Defused; Toribio submitted peacefully later in 1833

sources.citation: St. Pap., Missions and Colonization (C-A 53), tomo II, orig. pp. 215-234 / Savage 98-112, scan n97-n111, Doc 45 - Alferez Mariano G. Vallejo to the Comandante General (Figueroa), San Francisco, 5 May 1833, 'Informe reservado sobre el Establecimiento de Ross'.
sources.link_note: link probable, not confirmed by the record itself

sources.citation: St. Pap., Missions and Colonization (C-A 53), tomo II, orig. pp. 302-306 (Sav. p.462+) / Savage 214-220, scan n212-n218, Doc 115 - Jose Figueroa (Monterey) to the Ministro de Guerra y Marina, 12 Apr. 1833: founding of the strong detachment at Mission San Rafael and the Bodega/Russian rationale.

features.notes: Location approximate — the Bodega gathering ground, not a fixed engagement site. Two discrepancies I am NOT reconciling silently. (1) NAME: the map calls the Bodega chief 'Gualinela'; the C-A 53 record reads the Bodega capitanejo as 'Guchactac' (43 people, guarding the Russian factories). These may be the same man under different readings, or two different men; the catalog itself flags this document's paleography as rough and its figures as scale-2 abstracts pending verbatim transcription. Do not print either name as settled. (2) NAME: Toribio (Pixpix-uccux) does not appear in the catalog summary of ca53-d45 at all; the Indians 'resueltos a morir' are there, the leader's name is not. Toribio is named in Bancroft III:323 but only in the November 1833 Mercado episode, not in an April 1833 Bodega context. So the map's identification of the Bodega leader as Toribio rests on the underlying Vallejo report text, which has not been transcribed verbatim - treat it as unverified until the leaves are read. Also note the RAC manager at Ross in 1833 was Peter Kostromitinov, as the map says; the C-A record names only 'el Comandante' / Wrangel, so the Kostromitinov identification is an inference from the date, not from the document.

features.name: The Mercado Massacre at San Rafael
features.summary: After a 16 Nov parley — 15 gentiles under Toribio came to talk at Figueroa's encouragement, and Padre Vázquez del Mercado seized them following an overnight robbery — on the morning of 20 Nov 1833 Mercado sent majordomo Molina with 37 armed neophytes against the strangers: 21 killed, many wounded, 20 men, women, and children captured; the mission party lost 5 wounded, 1 mortally. Figueroa, indignant that his promises to the Indians had been broken, had Mercado suspended and summoned for trial; Vallejo freed the captives.
features.result: 21 gentiles killed; Mercado suspended; Vallejo freed the captives

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. III: 1825-1840 (San Francisco: A. L. Bancroft & Co., 1885), 322-324 and note 43.

features.name: Fight at Olómpali
features.summary: Ford's 'Bears' surprise Joaquín de la Torre's ~50 men (joined by Padilla's company) at breakfast at Camilo's rancho, midway San Rafael–Petaluma. First real fight of the revolt; one Californian killed.

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. V: 1846-1848 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), 164-168 ('Ford and Torre'; the fight at Olompali, 24 June 1846).

Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 31), tomo VII-VIII, orig. VII:250-254 / Savage 67-68, scan n70-n71, Doc 106 - Comandante general Jose Castro to Gov. Pio Pico, Santa Clara, 1 July 1846 (cited by Bancroft as Dept. St. Pap., MS., vii. 67-8).

features.notes: BEST FIND OF THIS BATCH: Bancroft cites this very document. At History of California V:167 n.18 (the running note on the crossing) he writes 'June 30th, Gen. Castro to Pico. Back at Sta Clara; and reports Torre's retreat and that of the other divisions (as explained in my text). A council of war has decided to send Manuel Castro as a comisionado to the gov... Blotter in Castro, Doc., MS., ii. 131. Same document, dated July 1st. Dept. St. Pap., MS., vii. 67-8.' Dept. St. Pap. vii. 67-8 is ca31-d106, whose Savage pages are exactly 67-68 - Bancroft was citing the Savage transcript's own pagination. Every other authority Bancroft uses for Olompali is non-C-A: Ford, Bear Flag, MS., 18-22; Baldridge, Days of '46, MS., 58-71; Larkin's Doc., MS., iv. 192, 202; Larkin, Off. Corresp., MS., i. 125; Ramon Carrillo's deposition in Hayes' Scrap-books; Luis German, Sucesos, MS., 18-24; Osio; Vallejo, Hist. Cal., MS., v. 129-33; the Honolulu Friend and the Monterey Californian. DISCREPANCY: the map says 'one Californian killed' - Bancroft's text gives Alferez Manuel Cantua killed and Agaton Ruiz badly wounded, while Larkin's 4 July letter names three casualties (Cantua, Ruiz, Isidoro) and Ramon Carrillo's deposition says 'one man killed and two wounded'. One killed is defensible but the count is contested in the sources.

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. V: 1846-1848 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), 171-173 ('A Murder by Fremont').
No Archives of California record found for the killing of the de Haro twins and Jose de los Reyes Berreyesa, 28 June 1846.
