Claims, 28; Jasper O'Farrell in the Los Angeles Star, 27 Sept. 1866 (the eye-witness for 'I have no room for prisoners'); J. S. Berreyesa's letter in the same paper; Leidesdorff to Larkin, 30 June, in Larkin's Doc., MS., iv. 189; Rico, Mem., MS., 19-23; Ide, Biog. Sketch, 190; Bidwell; Hargrave; Fowler, Bear Party, MS., 5; Martin, Narr., MS., 29; Chas Brown, Early Events, MS., 25-6. None is an Archives of California document. Content searches of the database ('de Haro hermanos muertos San Rafael estranjeros' restricted to 1846; 'asesinato Berreyesa Haro Fremont'; 'San Rafael estranjeros mataron tres' restricted to 1846) returned nothing on subject - the top hits were the Berreyesa land expedientes ca61-d259 / ca61-d260 and unrelated 1846 correspondence, and I have linked none of them. The likeliest explanation is that the Californio civil archive north of the bay had already collapsed: as Bancroft notes at V:239, subprefect Guerrero and comandante Sanchez had absented themselves and receptor Pinto had gone to join Castro, carrying his office archives off with him.

features.name: Capture of Monterey
features.summary: Sloat's squadron lands and raises the U.S. flag at the Custom House without resistance. The archive's own record: the landing general order bound into C-A 31, and the closing line 'Los Americanos han tomado á Monterrey.'

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. V: 1846-1848 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), ch. ix, 'Conquest by the U.S. - Sloat's Rule', 230-232 ('Taking of Monterey').

Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 31), tomo VII-VIII, orig. VII:261-262 / Savage 70-71, scan n73-n75, Doc 109 - John D. Sloat, commander U.S. naval forces in the Pacific, aboard the Savannah, 7 July 1846: landing orders to the squadron (in English), bound into the Californio archive.
Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 31), tomo VII-VIII, orig. VII:133-134 / Savage 34, scan n34, Doc 58 - Moreno to Stearns, San Luis Obispo, 11 July 1846, 'Toma de Monterrey - defensa de los Angeles - archivos'.
Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 31), tomo VII-VIII, orig. VIII:476-477 / Savage 138, scan n273, Doc 394 - David Alexander, San Pedro, 17 July 1846: the American squadron took Monterey by landing.

Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 31), tomo VII-VIII, orig. VIII:495 / Savage 146, scan n282, Doc 403 - Ignacio Coronel to his son Antonio Coronel, 1846: 'Los Americanos han tomado a Monterrey' - the volume's closing line.

Archives of California, Miscellaneous / Unbound Documents (C-A 63), Savage 211, scan n211-n213, Doc 313 - Acta de fidelidad al Gobierno Mexicano, Aduana Maritima de Monterey, 13 July 1846 (Pablo de la Guerra presiding; W. E. P. Hartnell and the guardas).

features.notes: Bancroft's ch. ix pages for the capture are 230-232. Sloat's summons of 7 July was delivered to the old artillery captain Mariano Silva, who replied that he had no authority to surrender and that there were no troops, arms or public property - which is why there is no Californio act of surrender in the archive to link to. The C-A holdings on this event are therefore of two kinds: the American landing order that Savage found bound into the Californio archive (ca31-d109), and the Californio reaction (ca31-d58, ca31-d112, ca31-d394, ca31-d403, ca63-d313). Note ca31-d109's record carries a published-record correction: its original page is VII:261-262, not the 281-2 given in an earlier publication.

features.name: Capture of Yerba Buena
features.summary: Montgomery lands from the Portsmouth and raises the flag on the plaza (now Portsmouth Square) without resistance.

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. V: 1846-1848 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), 238-239 ('The Stars and Stripes at San Francisco'), citing Montgomery's report to Sloat of the occupation of San Francisco, 9 July 1846, U.S. Govt Doc., 29th Cong. 2d sess., H. Ex. Doc. no. 4, pp. 649-50.
Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 31), tomo VII-VIII, orig. VII:266-269 / Savage 73-74, scan n77-n79, Doc 112 - Comandante general Jose Castro to Gov. Pio Pico, Los Ojitos, 11 July 1846, 'Incita a oposicion'.
sources.link_note: link probable, not confirmed by the record itself

sources.citation: No Archives of California record found for Montgomery's landing and the raising of the flag at Yerba Buena, 9 July 1846.

features.notes: There is a documentary reason for the gap, and it is worth putting on the map. Bancroft, V:239: 'Not only was there no opposition, but there was not in town a single Mexican official from whom to demand a surrender. Sub-prefect Guerrero and Comandante Sanchez had absented themselves; Port-captain Ridley was a prisoner at Sutter's Fort; and Receptor Pinto had more than a week before gone to join Castro, first disposing of the custom-house flag... and the archives of his office' - which Pinto later gave to Bancroft as the two-volume 'Documentos para la Historia de California. Coleccion del Sr Don Rafael Pinto' (a separate Bancroft Library collection, not C-A). So the Yerba Buena office archive that would have recorded the event was physically removed before it happened. Bancroft's own source is printed and American: Montgomery's report to Sloat of the occupation of San Francisco, 9 July 1846, in U.S. Govt Doc., 29th Cong. 2d sess., H. Ex. Doc. 4, pp. 649-50. Content searches run against the database: 'Yerba Buena bandera americana Montgomery' and 'San Francisco ocupado fuerzas americanas julio 1846' - no record of the landing or flag-raising.

features.name: Gillespie's capitulation at Los Angeles
features.summary: Flores's rising forces Gillespie's small garrison to capitulate and evacuate to San Pedro, reversing the first occupation of the south.

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. V: 1846-1848 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), 314-315 ('Los Angeles Retaken by the Californians') and notes 26-27.
No Archives of California record found for Gillespie's capitulation at Los Angeles, 29-30 Sept. 1846.

features.notes: NULL RESULT, recorded deliberately, and the null is itself the historical point: Bancroft, V:315, 'The terms of the capitulation, however, if they were put in writing at all, are not extant', and on the date, 'Gillespie says he marched to S. Pedro on Sept. 29th; Wilson thinks it was on the 28th; and several Californians make it the 30th. I find no document to settle it.' The map's 'Sept 29-30' is therefore correctly hedged. Bancroft's whole apparatus for the Flores revolt (V:311-315) is Californio and American dictation and correspondence, none of it C-A: Coronel, Cosas de Cal., MS., 80-107; Lugo, Vida de un Ranchero, MS.; Rico, Mem., MS., 25-35; Botello, Anales, MS.; Wilson's Observations, MS., 66-91; Forster's Pioneer Data, MS., 35-43; Vejar, Recuerdos, MS.; Michael White, Cal., MS.; Ord, Ocurrencias, MS., 184-5; Osio, Hist. Cal., MS., 480-5; Larkin, Off. Corresp., MS., ii. 89; Fitch, Doc., MS., 402; Manuel Castro to Pio Pico in Doc. Hist. Cal., MS., iii. 292. Content searches run: 'Gillespie capitulacion Angeles'; 'Flores pronunciamiento Angeles americanos septiembre' restricted to 1846; 'recuperacion de Los Angeles tropas americanas evacuar San Pedro'; 'Varela pronunciamiento 1846 Angeles guarnicion americana'; 'guerra Estados Unidos Angeles octubre' restricted to C-A 63 and 1846. Nothing on subject. The nearest C-A document from the resulting Flores government is ca63-d486, the Assembly's mission-mortgage war-loan decree of 30 Oct. 1846 - a month later and about finance, so I have NOT linked it.

features.name: Fight at Chino Rancho
features.summary: Californians under Varela/Carrillo besiege and burn Isaac Williams's rancho house, capturing ~24 Anglo-American riflemen (the 'Chino prisoners'). One Californian killed.

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. V: 1846-1848 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), pp. 311-314 ('was fought at the Chino rancho of Isaac Williams, about twenty-five miles east of Los Angeles, on September 26th-27th'; Carlos Ballesteros killed by a rifle-ball; Varela's promise of protection accepted).

Benjamin D. Wilson, 'Observations on Early Days in California', MS. (Bancroft Library dictation), 66-91 — Bancroft's principal source: 'Wilson's Observations, MS., is the most detailed and complete narration of the whole affair.'

José del Carmen Lugo, 'Vida de un Ranchero', MS. (Bancroft Library dictation), 32-67 (esp. 34 ff.) — Lugo claims to have arrived at Chino first and to have been joined by Varela late in the night; Bancroft: 'which was probably true.'

Stephen C. Foster, 'Los Angeles in 1847-49', MS. (Bancroft Library dictation), 25 ff.; Michael White, 'California All the Way Back to 1828', MS., 27-35; Francisco Palomares, 'Memorias', MS., 68-76 — the three supplementary participant/near-participant accounts of the assault and the sparing of the prisoners.
No Archives of California manuscript attests the fight at Chino.

features.notes: PAGE CORRECTION: Bancroft's account of the Chino fight runs pp. 311-314, not 311-313. The sentence begins on p.311 ('The first "battle" of this rebellion - or the second if we count Varela's demonstration against Gillespie -') and the surrender and march to Los Angeles occupy p.314. CROSS-FEATURE FINDING (applies to reg-132 through reg-140): I read Bancroft V continuously across the whole conquest narrative (the Flores revolt through Cahuenga, ch. xii-xiv, roughly pp. 305-408) and grepped that whole span for citations to any Archives of California series (Dept./Prov. St. Pap., Leg. Rec., Prov. Rec., Unb. Doc., 'Arch., MS.'). There is not one. Bancroft worked the conquest entirely from Bancroft-Library dictations, private document collections, and printed government reports. Independently, the C-A catalogue itself holds only TEN records dated between Aug 1846 and Jan 1847 across all 63 volumes, and none of them is military. That is the structural reason these nine features cannot be linked to C-A, and it is a real finding rather than a search failure.

features.name: Battle of Dominguez Rancho
features.summary: Mervine's ~350 sailors and marines, marching on Los Angeles without artillery, occupy the Dominguez rancho buildings overnight (7th), then are repulsed on the morning of the 8th by Carrillo's horsemen with the 'old woman's gun' pedrero fired by Ignacio Aguilar and dragged off by reatas to reload; ~4-6 Americans killed.

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. V: 1846-1848 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), pp. 318-320 ('Mervine's Defeat'; the gun 'fired by Ignacio Aguilar, and was immediately dragged away by reatas attached to the horsemen's saddles, to be reloaded at a safe distance').

José Antonio Carrillo, 'Accion de San Pedro contra los Americanos, 8 de Octubre 1846', MS. — the original official Californian report of the battle, dated at San Pedro 8 Oct. 1846; also printed in El Sonorense, 8 Jan. 1847.

Agustín Janssens, 'Documentos para la Historia de California', MS., 18-20 — Flores's congratulatory proclamation announcing the victory at San Pedro (and, at 45-6, the Flores order-book generally: 'among his papers are found many of Flores' orders not elsewhere extant').
No Archives of California manuscript attests the battle of Dominguez Rancho.

features.notes: Bancroft's page span is 318-320 (running heads: 'MERVINE'S DEFEAT. 319' and '320 REVOLT OF FLORES IN THE SOUTH'), with the narrative beginning at the foot of p.318; the existing citation's 319-321 is off by roughly a page. Also note that Bancroft's casualty figure is unsettled: Stockton said four killed, Cutts and most repetitions six killed and six wounded, Carrillo's own official report seven slain, Flores's report twelve, Gillespie thirteen. The map's '~4-6 Americans killed' sits at the low end of that range and is defensible but should not be stated as settled. The critical structural fact for this feature is Bancroft V:320: 'Archives of the Flores regime have for the most part disappeared; but enough remain in my collection from private sources to show the purport of the general's measures.' The surviving Flores paper is in Janssens's private papers, not in the C-A series.

features.name: Battle of Natividad
features.summary: Castro's/Manuel Castro's Californians fight Burroughs's and Thompson's volunteers near Natividad rancho, Salinas plain; Burroughs and Foster killed, ~5–7 dead total. The only pitched fight of the war in the north.

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. V: 1846-1848 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), pp. 367-372, ch. xiii ('Foster Killed - Battle of Natividad - Death of Burroughs').
José Antonio Alviso, 'Campaña de la Natividad', MS. (Bancroft Library dictation) — the son of the owner of the Natividad rancho, who claims to have first told Castro the Americans were at San Juan.
José Castro's contemporary report of the action, in [José] Fernández, 'Documentos', MS., 53 — 'In a report of the time, Castro claimed to have killed 21 of the enemy.'
No Archives of California manuscript attests the battle of Natividad.

features.notes: Bancroft's page span is 367-372 ('the Americans lost at Natividad four or five men killed' is on p.371; the chapter running head 'NATIVIDAD AND SANTA CLARA' covers 367-383). The map's casualty figure '~5-7 dead total' is within Bancroft's reported range but the testimony is irreconcilable and should be flagged rather than harmonised: American losses are given as 4 or 5 killed (Bancroft), Californian losses as 3 killed and 5 wounded (Castro's own report), 3 killed and 4 wounded (Vallejo), 4 killed and 4 wounded (Rico), 2 killed (Mrs Ord). Manuel Castro meanwhile claimed in a contemporary report to have killed 21 of the enemy, and Flores in December reported 11 Americans killed. Do not silently average these.

features.name: Battle of San Pascual
features.summary: Andrés Pico's lancers maul Kearny's dragoons in the San Pasqual valley at dawn; ~21 Americans killed including three officers — the bloodiest action of the war in California.

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. V: 1846-1848 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), pp. 342-347, ch. xiii ('The battle of San Pascual, the most famous and deadly in Californian history'; casualty roll and the lance wounds at n.27).

Capt. Andrés Pico's report of 6 Dec. 1846, received by Flores at 4 a.m. on 7 Dec. and communicated by him to subordinates, in Agustín Janssens, 'Documentos', MS., 45-6 — the victory won 'without other casualty on our side than 11 wounded, none seriously, since the action was decided por arma blanca.'

Dr John S. Griffin, 'Documents' / 'Papers', MS., 4-5 (original blotter of his quarterly report of 31 Dec. 1846) and 22 (letter of 14 Feb. 1847) — the assistant surgeon's own casualty returns, which Bancroft calls 'the best authority.'
No Archives of California manuscript attests the battle of San Pascual.

features.notes: CASUALTY DISCREPANCY, flagged not reconciled: the map says '~21 Americans killed'. Bancroft V:346 states eighteen killed in the fight, nineteen wounded of whom three fatally, and one missing. Counting the three who died of wounds (Hammond 6 Dec., Sgt Cox 10 Dec. at San Bernardo, Kennedy 21 Dec. at San Diego) plus the missing McLaffray gives 22; counting the fatally wounded but not the missing gives 21. The figure 21 is therefore defensible but is a derived total, not Bancroft's own number, and Bancroft records competing counts (Kearny 18 killed/15 wounded; Emory 18/13; House Ex. Doc. 17 killed/16 wounded; Griffin's original blotter 17/18). Andrés Pico's own report claims eleven wounded and no dead on the Californian side. The map's date (6 Dec. 1846) is not in dispute.

features.name: Pauma massacre
features.summary: Garra's band of Cahuillas and fugitive ex-neophytes of San Luis Rey kill eleven Californios who had retired to Pauma rancho to avoid service for or against Flores; instigated by William Marshall, later hanged for it.

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. V: 1846-1848 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), pp. 567-568 (the massacre of eleven men at Pauma rancho, Garra's Cahuillas and San Luis Rey fugitives, Marshall's instigation) and p. 617 (San Diego local annals: the roll of victims and the four competing explanations).
José Antonio Estudillo, 'Datos Históricos sobre California', MS., 45-6 — says the San Pascual Indians tried to save the victims but arrived too late.

Juan Machado [Alipás de Wrightington], 'Tiempos Pasados de la Alta California', MS., 37-42; Julio César, 'Cosas de Indios de California', MS., 11-14 (a Luiseño account); José del Carmen Lugo, 'Vida de un Ranchero', MS., 51-63 (the January 1847 Ahuanga counter-campaign) — the three Californio and Indian narratives of the massacre and its reprisal.
No Archives of California manuscript attests the Pauma massacre.

features.notes: COUNT DISCREPANCY, flagged not reconciled: Bancroft gives the number twice and inconsistently. At V:567 he writes 'the massacre of eleven men at Pauma rancho in December' (the map follows this); in his San Diego local annals at V:617 he names the victims and lists ELEVEN names plus 'a New Mexican not named' — i.e. twelve — and in the body of that annals passage he writes 'the massacre of a dozen Californians.' The named victims are Sgt Francisco Basualdo, José M. Alvarado, Manuel Serrano, Ramón Aguilar, Domínguez (known as Dominguito), an old man [unnamed], Santiago Osuna, José López, Santos Alipás, Eustaquio Ruiz, Juan de la Cruz, and an unnamed New Mexican. Bancroft also records four competing explanations of the killing and says 'there is much mystery about this affair' — including a theory, which he rejects, that there was no massacre at all and the men died at San Pascual. The map's attribution of instigation to William Marshall follows Bancroft, but Bancroft's own word is 'doubtless', an inference, and Marshall was hanged in 1852 after the Garra revolt, not immediately for Pauma.

features.name: Battle of Santa Clara ('the Mustard Stalks')
features.summary: Marston's marines and volunteers meet Francisco Sánchez's insurgents in the mustard fields near Mission Santa Clara; light casualties, followed by armistice ending the war in the north.
features.result: Sánchez treats; war ends in the north

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. V: 1846-1848 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), pp. 380-383, ch. xiii (the 'battle of Santa Clara'; the mustard growth at the creek crossing; the flag of truce that evening and the surrender of Sánchez on 8 January).

Henry Marshall, 'Statement', MS., 3-4 — the participant account Bancroft judges to narrate the affair 'briefly but with tolerable accuracy'; cf. Miguel Flores, 'Recuerdos', MS., 16-21, and Secundino Robles, 'Relación', MS., 19-25 (which Bancroft rejects as fiction).
William A. Richardson to Henry D. Fitch, 9 Jan. 1847, in Fitch, 'Documents for the History of California', MS., 411 — reports Bartlett's capture and the departure of Marston's force.
No Archives of California manuscript attests the battle of Santa Clara.

features.notes: SUBSTANTIVE CAUTION for the map text: the feature summary calls this a battle with 'light casualties'. Bancroft's finding is considerably more deflationary and should not be smoothed over — he concludes that Sánchez's men 'came for a few minutes within gunshot, and slightly wounded two of the Americans' and that 'no Californian was hurt', that Sánchez 'had no intention of risking a fight', and that the received accounts of a several-hour engagement with four or five Californians killed are inflations traceable to the Monterey Californian of 6 Feb. 1847 and to Charles Weber's self-serving 1880 reminiscence. Bancroft flatly calls Secundino Robles's detailed narrative 'pure fiction from beginning to end.' The map's 'light casualties' is compatible with Bancroft but 'two Americans slightly wounded, no Californian hurt' is what he actually establishes. Also: the armistice was agreed the evening of 2 Jan.; the surrender was concluded on 8 Jan. 1847, not on the 2nd.

features.name: Passage of the Río San Gabriel
features.summary: Stockton and Kearny force the river crossing against Flores's artillery and lancers ('Yankees at the crossing'); Californians withdraw toward the Mesa.

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. V: 1846-1848 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), pp. 392-394, ch. xiv (the passage of the Río San Gabriel, 8 January 1847; Emory's account of the charge on the left flank and the formation of squares).

Benjamin D. Wilson, 'Observations on Early Days in California', MS., 92 ff., and Juan Bautista Moreno, 'Vida', MS., 31-3 (Moreno commanded one of the charging companies and was seriously wounded) — the two closest Californian eyewitness manuscripts to the crossing.
California Historical Landmark No. 385, Battle of Río San Gabriel.
No Archives of California manuscript attests the passage of the Río San Gabriel.

features.notes: CHL No. 385 marker (NE cor. Washington Blvd & Bluff Rd, Montebello); battle at the river ford across present Whittier/Pico Rivera/Montebello. ⚠ NAME TRAP, documented so it is not repeated. The pre-computed candidate list offers ca31-d125 ('arranged transport of the mission's artillery pieces') and ca31-d203 ('reports the San Gabriel cannons are inservibles'), both 22 June 1846. These concern the ordnance of MISSION San Gabriel during Pico's June 1846 defensive scramble, six and a half months before, and have nothing to do with the January 1847 forcing of the Río San Gabriel crossing. They match on the place-name only and must not be linked. ca35-d1179 (Sept. 1847, custody of the San Gabriel mission buildings) is the same trap. I did not verify the CHL marker number (No. 385) independently; it is carried through from the existing citation.

features.name: Battle of La Mesa
features.summary: Final action: Flores's last attack on the American square on the plain south of Los Angeles fails; the pueblo reoccupied next day.

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. V: 1846-1848 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), pp. 395-397, ch. xiv ('About 4 o'clock the Californians retired, and the "battle of the Mesa" was at an end'; the flag of truce brought next morning by Célis, Ávila and Workman; the reoccupation of the pueblo at noon on 10 January).

A scrap in the handwriting of José Castro, in 'Documentos para la Historia de California', MS., i. 523: 'Mr Flores on this occasion hid himself in a little thicket of alders, and this was the only occasion when he saw the enemy.'

Dr Eversfield's casualty report in Griffin's 'Papers', MS., 18-19; Antonio F. Coronel, 'Cosas de California', MS., 80-107; Narciso Botello, 'Anales del Sur de la California', MS., 141 ff.; and Salvador Vallejo / Ávila, 'Notas Históricas', MS., 34 ff. — the surgeon's return and the three fullest Californian narratives.
California Historical Landmark No. 167, Battle of La Mesa.
No Archives of California manuscript attests the battle of La Mesa.

features.notes: CHL No. 167 marker (4490 Exchange Ave at Downey Rd, Vernon). CASUALTY NOTE, flagged: for the two days together (San Gabriel 8 Jan. and La Mesa 9 Jan.) Bancroft settles on three Americans killed and twelve wounded, against Stockton's own claim of three killed and fourteen wounded; the Californians lost three killed across both fights - Ignacio Sepúlveda, Francisco Rubio, and a Yaqui known as 'El Guaymeño' - with Capt. Juan B. Moreno and Alférez Ramírez the only named wounded. Stockton reported Californian losses 'between 70 and 80'; the printed Life of Stockton says over 70 killed and 150 wounded. Bancroft treats the American reports of enemy loss as worthless. The map's 'last Californio field action fails' is sound. I did not verify CHL No. 167 independently.

features.name: Capitulation of Cahuenga
features.summary: Andrés Pico surrenders to Frémont at the Campo de Cahuenga; generous terms end organized resistance in California.

sources.citation: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. V: 1846-1848 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), pp. 404-405, ch. xiv ('next morning, January 13th, it received the signatures of the respective commandants, Frémont and Pico'), with the seven articles and the additional article transcribed in full at n.20.

'Articles of capitulation made and entered into at the ranch of Couenga this 13th day of Jan., A.D. 1847', original seven articles with autograph signatures, in [José Antonio] Carrillo (D.), 'Documentos para la Historia de California', MS., 113-16 — in J. A. Carrillo's own hand, with the signatures to the additional article copied by him; a second copy from the original, including all articles, in Agustín Olvera, 'Documentos para la Historia de California', MS., 76.

Russell's receipt from Andrés Pico of 2 pieces of artillery with 6 charges of grape and 6 muskets, 16 Jan. 1847, in Olvera, 'Documentos', MS., 76-7; and the 18 Jan. Angeles blotter of six further articles proposed by Carrillo and Olvera under art. 7 of the treaty, in Olvera, 'Documentos', MS., 79-81.

Dept. State Papers, Miscellaneous / Unbound Documents (C-A 63), Savage p. 133 / scan n133–n134, Doc 236 — J. C. Frémont, Governor of California, to Juan Bautista Alvarado, Los Angeles, 26 February 1847: full pardon 'in the intention of contributing to the tranquillity of the territory by the return of its citizens to their families and homes… for any acts committed during the present hostilities against the Govt of the U.S.', with free passage and entire security of property and person.

features.notes: ⚠⚠ THE LOUDEST TRAP IN THIS BATCH. Five of the six pre-computed content candidates (ca36-d88, ca49-d1189, ca30-d230, ca30-d502, ca37-d310) are records of a CAHUENGA CAPITULATION — but of February 1845, the convention between Micheltorena and Castro that ended the Micheltorena war and expelled him from California. That is a different treaty, a different war, and a different pair of signatories, two years before Andrés Pico met Frémont. ca37-d310 is even headed 'CONVENCIÓN CELEBRADA ENTRE MICHELTORENA Y CASTRO'. Any of these linked to the January 1847 capitulation would be a serious, plausible-looking error. All five rejected. Note also that the Cahuenga articles are dated 13 Jan. 1847 but the additional article cancelling paroles and releasing all prisoners is dated at Los Angeles 16 Jan. 1847 — the map's single date of 13 January is right for the treaty proper.

features.name: Corsair squadron at Loreto
features.summary: Three English frigates (22–24 guns, 60–116 crew) anchor in the surgidero of Loreto — the capital itself — seizing a balandra, later ransomed for sugar, chocolate, and a church bell (~$8,000 losses). 'No dejan buque sin d[etener].'

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 14), tomo xxi. 68–9 / scan n17, Doc 17 — Arrillaga to the Viceroy, 16 June 1799: three frigates anchored in the surgidero of Loreto, the capital itself; they left behind the captured balandra; intelligence that the ships carry 22–24 cannon and 60–116 crew and that 'no dejan buque sin darle caza'; the Revolución under 'Juan Pivoré' expected.
sources.link_note: link probable, not confirmed by the record itself

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 14), tomo xxi. 69–70 / scan n18–n19, Doc 18 — report of Bernardo Juárez Infantzón, 27 June 1799: ransom of the balandra seized on 21 May, paid in sugar, chocolate and one church bell; losses about $8,000; the English held her from the 10th to the 16th.
sources.link_note: link probable, not confirmed by the record itself

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 14), tomo xxi. 70–2 / scan n19–n20, Doc 19 — Arrillaga to the Viceroy, 30 June 1799: 'la situación de la Península es muy triste, rodeada de buques ingleses, cuyos número no bajan de 4, y sin ningunos elementos de defensa'; the entire southern garrison is 8 soldiers, 1 cabo and 1 sargento; proposes a 50-man militia at 4 reales a day.
sources.link_note: link probable, not confirmed by the record itself

features.notes: BOTH EXISTING LINKS ARE WRONG AND ARE CORRECTED HERE. They are off by exactly nine document numbers in each case (d8→d17, d9→d18), which suggests a systematic slip rather than two independent errors — worth checking whether neighbouring 1799 Baja features on this map carry the same offset. Substantively: every phrase in the map's feature summary — 'three English frigates (22–24 guns, 60–116 crew)', 'anchor in the surgidero of Loreto — the capital itself', 'seizing a balandra, later ransomed for sugar, chocolate, and a church bell (~$8,000 losses)', and the quoted 'No dejan buque sin d[etener]' — is drawn from ca14-d17 and ca14-d18, not from the linked records. Two small points on the map text: the manuscript's phrase is 'no dejan buque sin darle caza' ('they leave no vessel unchased'), so the map's bracketed expansion '[detener]' should read 'darle caza'; and the balandra was seized on 21 May 1799, six weeks before the June anchoring at Loreto, so 'seizing a balandra' at Loreto slightly compresses the sequence — Doc 17 says the frigates 'left behind' the already-captured balandra.

features.name: Executions at Cabo San Lucas
features.summary: Four English corsairmen apprehended at Cabo San Lucas; the commander ordered three hanged. A Spanish brig on the Acapulco–San Blas run captured in the same campaign.

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 14), tomo xxi. 73–6 / scan n21–n22, Doc 21 — Arrillaga to the Viceroy, Aug./Sept. 1799: the English fleet of four frigates departs; four Englishmen apprehended at Cabo San Lucas, the commander ordering three of them hanged; a Spanish brig on the Acapulco–San Blas run captured in the same campaign.
sources.link_note: link probable, not confirmed by the record itself

sources.citation: Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 14), tomo xxi. 76–83 / scan n22–n25, Doc 22 — the Viceroy to Arrillaga, Sept./Oct. 1799: orders that no refuge be given to English ships and that disembarkation be prevented; Hidalgo supplies 20 muskets plus 15 from the Sutil; the 50-man militia approved and armed with 26 muskets; by 18 October, 67 men including 4 cabos and 3 sargentos under Sgt. Javier Aguilar.

features.notes: THE EXISTING LINK IS WRONG AND IS CORRECTED HERE — again a nine-document offset (d12→d21), matching the pattern in reg-141, which strongly suggests a single systematic mis-keying across the 1799 Baja corsair features rather than isolated slips. Substantively the record confirms the map on both points: four Englishmen apprehended at Cabo San Lucas, three of them hanged by the commander's order, and a Spanish brig on the Acapulco–San Blas run taken in the same campaign. One precision: the map heads the feature '1799' and Doc 21 is dated August/September 1799 at month confidence, so a firmer date than 'Aug.–Sept. 1799' is not available from this record. The record does not name the commander who gave the hanging order, nor the four Englishmen; do not supply names from elsewhere without a source.

features.name: Wilson's pursuit near San Bernardino
features.summary: Benjamin (Benito) Wilson with 200 mounted men pursues horse-raiding parties near San Bernardino; expedition diary filed, further campaign and remounts requested.

sources.citation: Dept. State Papers (C-A 30), tomo vi. 153–5 / Savage pp. 168–9 / scan n170–n171, Doc 277 — 'Diario de la expedición contra los indios', June 1845 [San Bernardino]: Comandante Benjamin (Benito) Wilson with 200 mounted men pursues the horse-raiding Indians near San Bernardino; skirmish at Los Naranjos in which Capitán Bahajes is wounded; the capitanejos submit.

Dept. State Papers (C-A 30), tomo vi. 147+ / Savage pp. 167–8 / scan n169–n170, Doc 276 — Miguel Pedrorena (Jamul) to the Government, 1 July 1845: 'Sobre expedición contra indios ladrones' — forwards the expedition diary, requires a further expedition and a caballada; captains Juan María González and José Bahajes.

features.notes: ⚠ DO NOT CONFUSE WITH THE 1846 EXPEDITION. The catalogue holds a second, later Wilson punitive expedition — ca31-d118, B. D. Wilson writing from Jurupa on 23 August 1846, 'Matanza de Indios', reporting his 22 August attack on a ranchería of the Amajaques. That is a different action, a year later, under a different government, and it must not be merged into this feature. DATE NOTE: ca30-d277 is dated to the month only (June 1845), so the feature's bare '1845' is correct and cannot honestly be sharpened from this record; the follow-up (d276) is 1 July 1845, which brackets the expedition as late June 1845. NUMBERS NOTE: '200 mounted men' comes straight from the manuscript abstract ('con 200 montados') and is Savage's summary of the diary's own claim, not an independent count. The map's 'raiders not destroyed' is a fair reading — the diary records a skirmish at Los Naranjos and the submission of the capitanejos, and d276 then asks for a further expedition, which implies the first did not settle the matter — but note the abstract also says Wilson 'somete á los capitanejos', so 'inconclusive' is a safer characterisation than 'failed'.
